## AI Agents for Business: When to Use One

An agent earns a place in your business only when the job branches and a person still checks the output. If the steps never change, write a plain workflow and stop there. Anthropic's December 2024 essay says to start with the simplest thing that works. It also splits a fixed workflow from an agent that picks its own tools.[^anthropic] We like that split, because vendors have blurred it for a year. Now even a reminder that fires the same way each time gets called an agent. That reminder is a workflow. An agent makes sense when the next step depends on what the last step found, and you cannot write every branch in advance. Even then a named person has to own the stop. An agent that nobody checks is just a risk with a nice name.

The [people guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-people-low) helps when the gap is who checks the work, not which model you rent. The [definition](/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) covers the words, in case they mean different things around your table. The [AI agent comparison](/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai) goes one step further, for when someone wants a fancier label than the job needs. Most owners we sit with do not need the label. They need one job held in place until a named person says it can go.

## Eight jobs, each with a stop

Inbox triage waits for a person before anything is sent. Meeting notes wait before they turn into tasks. Quote follow-up waits before a price goes out, and invoice questions wait before anyone promises a payment. Inventory exceptions wait before a purchase, and support replies wait before they reach the customer. Schedule changes wait before a customer is told, and a weekly report waits before anyone treats it as the record.

We would start from those eight and no others. Each one already happens in a shop, a clinic, or a trades office. Each one also has a moment when a wrong move hurts a customer or the books. If you use an agent, it gets the work ready and the person in the table below decides. If you cannot point at that person on a Tuesday, you do not have a real job yet. You have a demo.

<!--image:2-->

| Job | What the person still does |
| --- | --- |
| Inbox triage | Decides what is actually sent. |
| Meeting notes | Accepts the tasks. |
| Quote follow-up | Approves the price. |
| Invoice questions | Approves any promise to pay. |
| Inventory exceptions | Approves the order. |
| Support replies | Approves what the customer sees. |
| Schedule changes | Approves the message. |
| Weekly report | Accepts it as the record. |

<!--cta:inline-->

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.[^gartner-agentic] The reasons were cost, unclear value, and weak risk controls. Any job from the list with no named checker is a good fit for that pile. Cost grows when the agent keeps getting more systems because nobody drew an edge. Unclear value shows up when you cannot say which wait got shorter. Weak risk controls show up when the output goes out without waiting for anyone. A canceled project is not a moral failure. It is what happens to ideas that never became jobs. We would rather you skip a test than join that pile with a good story.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a clinic schedule, where an agent can be honest. The front desk owns the book, and the practitioner owns which visits are in scope. A patient asks to move a Tuesday visit later in the week. Whether that works depends on what the book shows and on whether that practitioner does that kind of visit. It also depends on a note that billing will need later. You cannot write every branch on a card, so someone has to look. An agent can look, draft the reply, and then wait. The front desk still approves the message, because some patients need a call and some need two plain sentences. The draft does not know the family. If the move changes the care plan, the practitioner signs off too. That is the stop, and it has a real name on it, not a switch that no job description mentions.

Now take the shop's weekly report. People like to call it an agent job because the word sounds busy. The report has the same shape every time, with yesterday's sales, the items that ran low, and the invoices still open. Nothing in it depends on a find that changes the next step, so a plain workflow can build it. A person then accepts it as the record, or it stays a draft. If you buy an agent for that job, you pay for judgment you did not need. You also skip the judgment you did need, which is the bookkeeper deciding if the numbers are right. Until she does, the report is a rumor in a nice font.

A trades desk shows both shapes in one afternoon. Quote follow-up branches when a customer asks a question that changes the price. The agent can pull the old notes and draft a reply, but the owner approves the price before anything goes out. Invoice questions are stricter. A promise to pay is never the agent's to make, so the person approves any promise. Inventory exceptions wait before a purchase, since the wrong part costs a truck trip. Support replies wait before the customer sees them. Schedule changes wait before anyone says the van is coming, and meeting notes wait before they become tasks the lead tech never agreed to. Inbox triage waits before anything is sent, even the cheerful draft that was about to go to the wrong thread. None of this needs a new department. All of it needs the wait to be real, because a wait that means "someone usually glances at it" is only a wish.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job as if it were a plain workflow. Say who starts it, what they make, and who gets it. If you can finish that page without a branch, ship the workflow and stop. Anthropic's advice to start simple is the whole method here. An agent is an exception you earn, not a default you announce.

Second, circle the step where the next action depends on what you found. On the clinic book, the next message depends on the open slots and on whether the visit is in scope. On quote follow-up, the next sentence depends on whether the customer's question changed the job. If you cannot circle a step like that, you have circled a feeling. A feeling does not make a project.

Third, if you did circle one, name the person who approves, and treat the table as the least you do. Use the name of the actual person at your desk, not a role like operations. If that person is "whoever is free," you have already described the cancellation. Free people rarely check the work, but named people do, even on their grouchiest mornings.

Fourth, decide what wrong looks like before you turn anything on. It might be a visit moved to the wrong day or a price the owner never said. It might be a payment promise the bookkeeper would not make, or a draft report treated as the books. The risk control is that list plus a place where the output sits until someone checks it. Gartner's reasons are not abstract here. Weak risk controls just mean a send button with no waiting room.

Fifth, run one job from the list and leave the rest with a person, the old way. Inbox triage or schedule changes are enough to start. Do not light up quote follow-up, support replies, and the weekly report all at once. Give the job one branch, one checker, and one week of real messages. If the checker starts to skip the wait because the draft is usually fine, you have learned something useful. Usually fine is how the wrong message leaves the building.

Sixth, come back to the list only when the first job feels dull. That means the person still checks, the branch still matters, and you can say what value showed up without making up a chart. If you cannot, turn it off before cost becomes the reason someone else does. Ending a small test is a win. Feeding it until the hype fades is how that canceled pile gets its next member.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is calling every automation an agent, and the vocabulary notes exist to stop it. A fixed sequence that files a photo and waits for a price is a workflow. It can be excellent, but it does not get better when you rename it. We have watched owners pay an agent premium for a checklist and then feel cheated when it acted like a checklist. The checklist was honest, and the brochure was not.

Letting the output send itself is the mistake that reaches a customer. The table is blunt on purpose. Someone decides what is sent, someone approves what the customer sees, and someone approves the schedule message. Take those lines out and a confident drafter holds the keys. Confidence is not permission. The front desk knows who needs a phone call, and that knowledge will not be in the prompt you wrote on a calm afternoon.

Starting from the model instead of the branch is how tests turn pricey and vague. Someone wants "an agent for the business" the way they might want a new hire with no desk. But there is no seat called the business. There is inbox triage, or there is not. There is a weekly report that someone must accept, or there is a PDF that will be quoted as fact. Pick a row. If none of the rows hurt this month, you have curiosity and not a project. So read the definition post and hold off on a platform deal.

Ignoring the forecast because it sounds like a big company's problem is how small firms get a smaller version of the same ending. Over 40% is not weather that only hits large firms. Cost, unclear value, and weak risk controls fit a clinic or a trades desk just as well. Your version will not make the news, but it will make a monthly bill and a queue of drafts that nobody trusts. You do not need a bigger disaster to take the warning.

Giving the check to a committee is a polite way to have no checker. "Someone will review it" means the draft sits there until it does not. Write one name, and give that person the power to say no without a meeting. If the job matters enough for an agent, it matters enough for a name. If it does not matter enough for a name, it does not matter enough for an agent.

## What we'd do

We would start with a workflow and make the agent earn the exception, even when the demo is charming. A charming demo is not a branch. A real branch is a schedule change that alters what you may say, or a customer question that changes a price. If we cannot see that in a real job from last week, we ship the fixed path and go home. Going home is a fine result, because not every visit should end with a new system.

We would put a person's name on the check before anything is turned on, and we would treat the table as a contract. The person decides what is sent and accepts the tasks. The person approves the price, any promise to pay, and the order. The person also approves what the customer sees and the schedule message, and accepts the report as the record. If a proposal will not attach a name to the row you picked, that is the missing risk control showing up early. Believe it.

We would not run the whole list just to feel modern. One job held at the stop beats eight half-starts that get canceled for the reasons Gartner already gave. If you want a test this week, pick schedule changes or inbox triage and write down the name of the approver. Then refuse every extra system until that person has lived with the wait. You can add the agent once the wait is real. It does not get to create the wait by existing.

## AI Agents vs Agentic AI: A Plain Split

An AI agent directs its own tools toward a goal. "AI that takes actions on its own" is the wider label for many of those systems across a company. The words get sold as if they were the same purchase, but they are not.

In Anthropic's December 2024 essay, an AI agent is a system that directs its own tools toward a goal.[^anthropic] A workflow is the opposite, because its steps are written in advance. The wider label is what vendors use when they mean many such systems, often spread across a company. We repeat the split often. A deck will use the big word for a single inbox rule, and the owner walks out thinking they bought a workforce.

The [definition](/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) is the short version of the split between a path you wrote and a model that chooses. The [jobs list](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) shows where one agent might actually sit. The [people guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-people-mid) covers who has to check the output. If you cannot name that person, the rest of the vocabulary does not matter yet.

## What the forecast says

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of AI projects that take actions on their own will be canceled by the end of 2027.[^gartner-agentic] The reasons are cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. Read those reasons as a checklist you can fail on purpose. A project with no named job will look unclear, and a project nobody can halt will look like a risk problem. A project that needs three new tools and a consultant to explain them will look expensive, and then it will stop.

The same note said 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made on their own by 2028, up from 0% in 2024. It also said 33% of enterprise software will include this kind of AI by 2028, up from less than 1% in 2024. Hold both forecasts at once. A lot of software will grow an agent feature, and a large share of the projects that chase the label will be canceled. A feature that arrives in a product you already pay for is a different event. A program you start because the word showed up on a board slide is another thing.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

If you can write the steps, you want a workflow. If the next step depends on what the last step found, you may want an agent, and you still want a person who can stop it. A bigger label does not change that checkpoint.

We use the forecast as a brake and not as a scare. Projects get canceled when the job was never clear enough to survive a budget meeting. They also get canceled when the risk control is a sentence in a policy that nobody on the desk has read. You can avoid both without giving up the tool. Name the decision and name the checker, and keep the wider program on the shelf until that pair has worked on real afternoons.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk a small clinic with us. This is a scene and not a study, so it has no score attached. Nora owns the practice, one person runs the front desk, and Dr. Patel sees patients. The phones pile up after lunch. Most callers want to know whether a symptom can wait, whether a form was received, or whether tomorrow's visit is still on.

A workflow can carry the parts that do not change. A missed call becomes a task, and the form either arrived or it did not. A reminder goes out the afternoon before, with the address and what to bring. The front desk lead already does this by hand. Writing it down does not need a new kind of software. It needs the front desk lead's order, and a screen that will not skip the "what to bring" line when the day gets rude.

An agent is the narrower ask. A patient writes that the rash spread and that they also have a fever, and they want to know if they should come in today. The next step depends on what the note says. A model could draft a reply that offers the urgent slot and says what to watch for, using only the phrases Dr. Patel has approved. The front desk lead still sends it, and Dr. Patel still owns anything that sounds like a diagnosis. The agent picked its tools, which were the template and the schedule, and stayed inside its bounds. That is one agent, and it is not a whole program.

The bigger bet is what gets pitched on sales calls. One system talks to the schedule, another drafts the chart note, another chases the referral, and another updates the billing code. They hand work to each other while Nora is with a patient. That is the shape of the projects in the cancellation forecast. Cost shows up as four subscriptions and a person whose job becomes watching them. Value stays unclear because nobody can say which decision got better. Risk control fails the first time a draft hints at a diagnosis and leaves the building. We would not start there. We would start with the front desk lead's reminder path. Then we would add one draft for the fever note, with the send step still done by a person.

The roles are the point of the walk-through. Nora decides which phrases are allowed. The front desk lead is the checker who can throw a draft away, and Dr. Patel is the only person who closes a clinical question. A vendor who cannot point at those three seats is selling a category and not a checkpoint. That goes double when the vendor calls the whole bundle by a bigger name because it sounds larger.

## How we'd run it

We would separate the words on a single page before anyone signs an order.

First, write the job as one decision. For example, "Reply to a same-day symptom note with an approved phrase, or book the urgent slot." The rule is to never invent a diagnosis. If the job is "make the clinic smarter," throw it out and start again.

Second, list the steps the front desk lead already does that never change. Log the call, check the form, send the reminder, and hold the chart for the clinician. That list is a workflow, so build it. Do not wait for a platform to find it for you.

Third, circle the one place where the next step depends on what the message says. A symptom plus a fever is a fork, but a reminder is not. The fork is the only candidate for an agent, and everything else stays on the path you wrote.

Fourth, write the bounds in the front desk lead's own language. The agent may use the approved phrases and the urgent column on the schedule. It may not name a condition, promise a medication, or tell someone to stay home. If a phrase is not on the card, the draft does not use it.

Fifth, name the checker on the rota and not in a policy file. That is the front desk lead on desk days and the backup coordinator when the lead is out. Dr. Patel covers anything the card does not. The stop rule is simple. If the draft has no fever detail, or the message is angry, or a phrase is not on the card, the draft is thrown away.

Sixth, run last week's real messages with the names removed. Nora and the front desk lead mark the drafts they would have refused. Fix the card until the refusals match their judgment, and only then let it draft against today's inbox. The checkpoint is the same whatever you call the system.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is using the wide word for a narrow tool. A reminder sequence is a workflow, and a chatbot that waits for a person to paste a question is one prompt. Neither one is a system of actors because the proposal says so. The staff then expects a team of helpers and gets a mail merge.

The second mistake is starting with the whole constellation. That means several tools and several handoffs, with nobody who can draw the path on a whiteboard. Gartner expects a large share of projects like that to be dropped by the end of 2027, for cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. A clinic does not need to donate itself to that share.

The third mistake is treating the 2028 lines as a deadline for your front desk. The 15% of work decisions made on their own and the 33% of software with this kind of AI are statements about a market. They are not a due date for Nora. Software you already own may grow a new feature, and you still choose whether the front desk lead is allowed to rely on it.

The fourth mistake is a checker who exists only on paper. "The clinical lead reviews outputs" means nothing on a Tuesday when the lead is in a room and the draft is in the outbox. If the person who can stop it is not at the desk, you do not have the control. You have a sentence.

The fifth mistake is letting a draft sound like Dr. Patel. Patients do not hear "language model" when a message arrives. They hear the clinic. A warm sentence that implies a diagnosis is a clinical act, so keep it off the card and throw away any draft that sneaks one in.

The sixth mistake is buying because 0% feels embarrassing. The note said that decisions made on their own sat at 0% in 2024, which is a baseline and not an insult. Moving off it without a named decision is how the cancellation reasons show up in a smaller budget.

## What we'd do

We would buy the workflow first and the single agent second, and we would leave the big program unsold. Our view is that the wider word is doing sales work. It makes a reminder bot sound like a strategy, and it makes a careful one-agent test sound small. Small is the right size until the front desk lead can refuse a draft without calling a vendor.

If the next step truly depends on what the note found, we would use one agent, one card of phrases, and one person who can stop it. If the steps can already be written, we would stay with the workflow. Then we would spend the money on the afternoon when the front desk lead is underwater. The June 2025 forecast is not a reason to hide from the tool. It is a reason to refuse a project that cannot name its checker. We would rather be the clinic that canceled nothing, because we never started the project that deserved canceling.

## AI Automation Agency vs Consultant: Who to Hire

Hire a consultant to name the job, and hire an agency only after that naming is done. An AI consultant names the job, the data, and the stop. An automation agency builds the system once those three are written down. When the agency comes first, the build has no owner. We've watched that happen in the wrong order more than once. The proposal arrives with staff, a toolset, and a start date. Nobody in the room can say which output a person still has to check. The build goes ahead anyway, because the calendar was the only decision anyone made.

The [consultant note](/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business) is the list of questions we wish owners had before the first sales call. The [buy-or-build note](/blog/off-the-shelf-ai-or-custom-software) covers whether to build at all. The [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-mid) gives you a matching score when the choice itself is the thing you keep putting off. Hiring is a decision, so score it before you sign. A signature on a vague scope is not a plan. It is a hope with a payment schedule.

## Two training figures, two populations

Microsoft's 2024 index says only 25% of companies were planning to offer generative AI training.[^microsoft] Statistics Canada's 2025 report says 38.9% of Canadian businesses that already use AI had trained staff.[^statcan] Those are different groups of people, so do not average them. One is a plan among companies. The other is training that already happened at businesses using AI. A pitch that blends the two into "about a third of firms train people" has invented a fact. Planning and doing are not the same thing. Companies and AI-using businesses are not the same group. The two surveys also cover different countries and different years. If a consultant or an agency treats them as one number, they are not reading the reports. They are decorating a slide.

<!--image:2-->

McKinsey's 2025 survey says 23% are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, and 39% are still experimenting.[^mckinsey] An agency pitch that quotes only a usage figure is selling the experiment. Experimenting is the larger group, and rolling out somewhere is the smaller one. The word "somewhere" matters here. It does not mean the job you care about or a firm the size of yours. We bring this up because the word agent shows up in proposals early. Nobody admits they are still testing. An experiment can be the right buy if it is labeled as one, with a stop and a person. An experiment sold as a finished operation is how an owner ends up maintaining a demo.

<!--cta:inline-->

Pay a consultant to refuse work that a product already does. Pay an agency when the process is written and the checker has a name. The refusal is the valuable part, and it is the part a build contract is bad at. A builder is paid to build, but a consultant can be paid to say don't. If you only hire people who get paid when the project starts, you will get a project. You may not get a job worth doing.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a clinic that almost hired an agency to put an AI agent on the front desk. This is a walkthrough, not a scoreboard. The owner had three calls in one week and a folder of proposals. The front desk still books by phone and by a form on the site. The practitioner still decides which visits are in scope. Billing still waits for a note that the visit happened. Ask what the agent would be allowed to send and the room goes quiet. Ask what happens when the draft is wrong and the room gets quieter. That quiet is the consultant's whole job. It is to name the work, the data it may see, and the stop.

In that room we would send them to a consultant before any build. The consultant's output is a page, not a login. The page might say that the front desk drafts reminders and a person sends them. It might say the practitioner is the stop whenever a reminder includes a clinical instruction. It might say billing is not part of this job at all. It might also say the booking product they already pay for sends a plain reminder. Then they should not build one. That refusal is worth more than a sprint of work. An agency that starts before the page exists will build the reminder anyway. A reminder is easy to demo. Easy to demo does not mean it was missing.

A trades desk is the other shape, and it is where an agency can be the right call. The quote steps are already written. The office manager logs the address, and the lead tech files measurements before leaving the driveway. The owner sets the price, and that price is the stop. The bookkeeper does not open an invoice until the yes is written down. A product they tried does not keep site photos and supplier notes in one place. The checker has a name, so this is a real build. Even then we would want the agency to repeat the stop back to us. They should do it before they give an estimate. If they talk about agents and never say the owner's name next to the price, they are selling an experiment. It is the same one that McKinsey's larger group is still running.

A small shop is usually neither a big consulting story nor a custom build. The owner wants someone to do AI because a neighbor did. The clerk already knows the reorder, and the bookkeeper already keeps a late-invoice list. A consultant who earns the fee will point at one of those jobs, refuse the rest, and go home. An agency will only earn a fee here if one job truly needs a system that no product covers. Most weeks, it does not. Paying either of them to rediscover the clerk's list is a polite way to avoid deciding.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job in one sentence that a new hire could read. Do not write "AI for the front desk." Write "The front desk sends appointment reminders after a person reads them." If you can't get to a sentence like that, you are hiring a mood. Moods get expensive when they come with a team.

Second, write down the data the job may touch and the data it may not. Reminders can see the time and the place. They can't see the clinical note unless a named practitioner says so. Quotes can see the site measurements, but they can't invent a price. If the data line says "whatever the model needs," you don't have a boundary. You have a hope that the vendor will be careful. Vendors are careful about their own scope, so you have to be careful about yours.

Third, name the checker in the same sentence as the job. That means a person, a place where the output waits, and what happens if it is wrong. A checkpoint nobody owns is not a checkpoint. We would rather delay the hire than sign a scope where "someone will review it" is the only human. Someone is not a name, and when everyone is responsible, everyone goes home.

Fourth, ask whether a product already does this work. The consultant is paid to refuse it. If the booking tool already sends the plain reminder, stop there. If the books already flag the late invoice, stop there too. Bring in an agency only for the gap that remains after that refusal. The buy-or-build note is the longer version of this step. Don't skip it because an agency proposal looks nice.

Fifth, keep the training story apart from the build story. The 25% figure is companies planning to offer training. The 38.9% figure is AI-using businesses that had trained staff. Neither one promises that your clerk will be shown the new way of working. Put the training in the scope. A launch with nobody to run the job next Tuesday just moves the work back into the owner's memory. That is where it already lived.

Sixth, if the proposal mentions agents, ask whether they are rolling out or experimenting. Make them pick one. The 23% and 39% figures are not invitations. They are a warning about language. If the honest answer is experiment, write "experiment" at the top of the scope. Add a date when you will decide to keep it or turn it off. If they can't say, you are buying a word.

## Common mistakes

Hiring the agency because the proposal had more pages is the mistake with the nicest paper. Pages are not a named job, and a bench of people is not a checker. We've sat with owners who chose the thicker folder because it felt serious. Seriousness is a person who will tell you not to start. The thinner conversation is often the one that saves the quarter, and we don't mean a cheap one. We mean a conversation that is allowed to end in no.

Averaging the training figures is the mistake that makes everyone sound informed. Someone says firms don't train. Someone else quotes the other survey as if it were the same study, and the room nods. They are not the same study. One is a plan in a 2024 index of companies. The other is training already done among Canadian businesses that use AI, in a 2025 report. Use either number alone with its group, or use neither. The fake average will be repeated to your staff as if it were a law. It is not one.

Buying the experiment under a rollout headline is how agent talk gets into a clinic that only needed a reminder. McKinsey's split helps if you say it out loud in the meeting. Most of the people in that survey were not rolling out an agent system anywhere. If your seller quotes only a usage number, ask what happened to the people who were still experimenting. Then ask which group the proposal belongs to. Silence is an answer, so treat it as one.

Leaving the refusal out of the contract is how you pay twice. You pay the agency to build the thing the product already did. Then you pay the product to keep doing it. A consultant who won't refuse is a salesperson with a notebook. We would rather pay for a no on a single page. A yes that copies the booking tool costs more. Put the right to stop in writing before the build gets a channel and a weekly call.

Skipping the owner of the output is the last mistake, and it survives all the others. The scope names a platform but does not name the office manager. On the first real day the draft is ready and nobody's job includes looking at it. The agency did what it was paid to do. The consultant, if you had one, either wasn't heard or wasn't asked. The draft waits in a queue that counts as a success on paper. Customers never see the success. They see whatever got out.

## What we'd do

We would hire the namer first, almost every time. We would pay them to be willing to end the work with a refusal. That is our opinion. A clinic that can't say what the front desk may send doesn't need an agency yet. A shop whose late invoices already live in the bookkeeping product doesn't need either one. A trades desk is the rare room where we would call a builder. The steps are written, a named person owns the price, and no product covers the gap. Even there, the builder does not get to rename the job.

We would not let a single training statistic into a proposal without its group sitting next to it. We would not let "agent" into the scope unless someone can show the step that branches. We would also want to meet the person who stops it. We would not sign a start date that arrives before the page. Dates are easy, but pages are the work. If the seller needs the date to keep their staff busy, that is their problem. They can solve it after you know what you are buying.

If you only do one thing before the next call, write the sentence with the job and the checker. Then ask the seller to repeat it without adding a platform. If they can't, you are not late. You are early, which is the right time to be early. The experiment will still be there next month. Your name on a vague scope is much harder to take back.

## AI Automation for Small Business: Which Job First

AI automation for a small business starts with one choice. You pick which job goes first. You do not shop through a long list of tools. We score each job on four things, in plain words. How often does the job happen? How steady are the rules? Can a computer read the data? What does it cost when the answer is wrong? A job that happens a lot, follows steady rules, has readable data, and is cheap to fix belongs first. A rare choice with a costly mistake does not, however shiny the demo looked.

The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) is where we ask the work to show us its slow spot. The [mapping note](/blog/business-process-automation-ai) covers the step before any tool, when the job is still a story in someone's head. The [agency note](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) is about hiring, which comes after you know the job. If you hire first, you get sold a stack of tools. The stack was never the real choice.

Owners often tell us they want automation the way a person wants a clean garage. They want the feeling of less mess. That feeling does come, but only after one ugly, repeated job gets a written path to follow. A long menu of features will not bring it.

## What the surveys already count

Statistics Canada found that in the second quarter of 2025, 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services. A year earlier it was 6.1%.[^statcan] Among the businesses that used AI, 35.7% used text analytics and 23.1% used marketing automation. Also, 40.1% had built new ways of working, and 38.9% had trained their staff. We read that as a list of jobs people tend to start with. We do not read it as a score of how well you are doing. Sorting text shows up, and so does marketing that can be counted. New ways of working and trained people show up right beside the tool, which is the part sellers mention last.

<!--image:2-->

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI. That is up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] It is a different question. Opening a tool that writes text for you is not the same as putting AI inside the way you deliver your product. A shop can sit inside the Chamber number and outside the Statistics Canada number on the same afternoon. If a seller quotes only the bigger share, ask them for the smaller one too. The smaller one is closer to the job you are about to change.

<!--cta:inline-->

We would read the Statistics Canada list as a plain line of jobs to pick from. You can sort text, run marketing that you can measure, write a new way of working, and train the people who will run it. Try the four-part test on each one before you buy anything. A job that fails the test can still be done by a person. That is not a loss, because it means the test did its work.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Picture the counter of a small company that sells parts to repair shops. This is only a walk-through. We are not claiming a result that we measured. The owner still knows the odd customers by their voices. A bookkeeper posts invoices three mornings a week, and a floor lead pulls the orders. Someone, often the owner's niece, looks after social media, mostly by feeling bad about it.

Three piles sit on the desk, and only one of them deserves a machine.

The invoice pile is dull and never ends. Vendors send scans, and the lines repeat from one scan to the next. The rules are boring and mostly steady. The job is to match the vendor, match the amount, and flag a duplicate. It must never make up a category that the bookkeeper has not approved. A computer can read the scan if it is clear. When it cannot, a person still has the paper. A wrong suggestion only costs a quick fix before anything is posted, as long as the bookkeeper is the one who posts. This pile passes the test, so it is the job we would touch first.

The social pile looks easier, but it is a worse first job than people think. The niece can already write a caption with a tool that makes text. That is the Chamber kind of use, and it is fine. Marketing automation is a real group among the businesses that already use AI, as the Statistics Canada numbers show. Still, it fails our test when nobody knows what a good post is for. It also fails when the product names keep changing because the floor lead hears them wrong. The volume is low and the rules are mushy. A wrong caption is usually cheap to fix, but cheap is not enough when the other parts wobble. We would leave it as a draft that a person writes.

The third pile is a furious one-off. A repair shop says a part failed and wants a credit, a lecture, and a promise. The rules are not steady, because the relationship is the rule. The facts are a phone call, a photo, and ten years of memory in the owner's head. A wrong reply could cost the account. This job fails on purpose, and we would not automate the apology. We would let the owner make it. We would keep the tool away from that thread, so it cannot sound smooth and still be wrong.

We would put the bookkeeper in charge of the invoice test. She knows a duplicate when she sees one, and the niece and the owner do not. The floor lead's job is to say when a vendor name on the scan is the warehouse nickname and not the legal name. The owner's job is to say no when someone wants to add the angry-customer job while they are at it. That refusal is the whole plan.

## How we'd run it

We run the choice like a filter. Anything that gets through can become a small setup. Anything that does not stays manual, and there is no shame in that.

First, we list the possible jobs in the owner's own words on one page, with no tool names. That might be invoices, captions, the angry credit, and a mailbox full of questions about whether you have a certain part. Then we ask which one happens even when everyone is tired, because the tired job is usually the right one. Rare, heroic jobs attract software, and then the software sits unused.

Second, we score each job on the four tests, out loud, with the person who does the work. We ask how often it happens and how steady the rules are. We ask whether a computer can read the source or whether the source is just a memory. We also ask what a wrong answer costs. Can a named person catch it before it leaves? The invoice passes, the caption is a maybe that we set aside, and the credit fails. We write the fails down so they do not creep back into the plan later as a second phase.

Third, we map the job that passed before we look at any products. That map is what the [mapping note](/blog/business-process-automation-ai) is about. We ask who touches the scan and where it is saved. We ask what the bookkeeper changes by hand and what she refuses to let a suggestion decide. If we cannot draw that with her, we are not ready to buy. The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) helps here when the owner insists every job is equally slow. It is not, and one of them is eating the whole morning.

Fourth, we pick a tool only after the map exists, and we like the dull tool that fits the map. A tool that reads the scan and offers a guess the bookkeeper can reject is plenty. We do not add a bot that talks to customers just because the invoice project feels too plain to brag about. Plain is the point. If the owner wants help choosing who should build or advise, that talk waits until now. It belongs with the [agency note](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) and not at the start.

Fifth, we train the person who will run it, and we call the project unfinished until she is trained. Statistics Canada found that among businesses that used AI, 38.9% had trained staff and 40.1% had built new ways of working. Those are not extras next to the 12.2% that used AI in production. They are the reason production use is still the smaller number. We would rather wait to switch it on than hand the bookkeeper a login and a wish.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is starting from a tool menu, which is what the catalogs push you to do. The menu lists marketing, chat, and invoices, along with a promise that they all share one brain. Your desk does not share one brain. The invoice rules are steady and the angry customer is not. If you buy the bundle just because it comes bundled, you bring a failing job in alongside a passing one.

The second is treating generative use as automation, which is the Chamber trap. The 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. The niece who writes a caption may already be in that crowd. She has not automated the way you deliver anything. If you tell yourself that you automated marketing, you will skip the bookkeeper, who was the real chance.

The third is automating a rare and costly choice because it hurts. That is a mistake of feeling more than of thinking, because pain is not a test. The credit argument hurts, so the owner wants it gone. But gone in software means a smooth reply that might be false. That kind of mistake is not cheap to catch, so we leave it with a person.

The fourth is skipping training because the screen looks friendly, which is how a new way of working dies. A friendly screen still has a reject button that nobody was taught to trust. Among the businesses already using AI, 38.9% had trained staff. That is not a high bar, and many still miss it. We would miss it too if we let the launch meeting turn into a tour of buttons.

The last is copying another company's first job. Their text sorting might be sacred while yours is a mess of photos. Their marketing might be a weekly habit while yours is guilt. The surveys describe crowds, and the four tests describe your morning. Use the crowd for ideas, and use your morning to decide.

## What we'd do

We would put the invoice, or your version of the repeated and readable pile, ahead of every shinier idea. That is our opinion. In the Statistics Canada count, text analytics made up 35.7% of the uses among businesses that used AI, and marketing automation made up 23.1%. Both are fair choices. We still start where the bookkeeper can catch a wrong line before any money moves. Marketing drafts can wait in the niece's hands, checked by a person, until the rules are plain enough to write down.

We would not let the Chamber's 58% set the pace. That number, and the climb from 23% in 2023 to 40% in 2024, says that generative tools are spreading. It does not say your delivery should be handed to one. The production number is the stricter crowd. It was 12.2% in the second quarter of 2025, up from 6.1% a year earlier. Join it with one job, a new way of working, and a trained person. Or do not say that you joined.

If you are unsure which pile is eating your week, open the [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) and let the slow job show itself. Then map it with the [mapping note](/blog/business-process-automation-ai) before you talk to a builder. When you do need a person, the [agency note](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) will keep you from hiring a whole platform when you only needed a checker. We would rather automate one dull pile well than say you run on automation while the bookkeeper still retypes every scan.

## AI Consultant for Small Business: What to Ask

A useful AI consultant for a small business can name the job, the data, and the person who is allowed to stop the work. If a ready-made product already does that job, the honest advice is to buy the product and skip the custom project. We would rather lose the work than invent a build to justify a fee. That is how the [studio](/) works. If you are torn between a consultant and a firm that wants to own the install, read the [agency comparison](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant). If a pretty first test run never became a real process, read the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall).

Bring the person who does the job into the first meeting. An owner alone will be sold a platform. The office manager, the bookkeeper, or the dispatcher will ask where the file lives. That question is worth more than any slide with a diagram. If the consultant looks annoyed by it, you have learned something cheap.

We feel strongly about this because we have watched the other way go wrong. A pitch that starts with a tool name has skipped the work. You can always get back to a tool later. You cannot easily get back the month you spent building the wrong promise.

## What gets canceled

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. It named cost, unclear business value, and weak risk controls as the reasons.[^gartner-agentic] In a poll of 3,412 people, 19% said their group had made big investments in AI agents. Another 42% had made small ones, 8% had made none, and 31% were waiting or unsure. Gartner also said only about 130 vendors sold what it would call a real AI agent. Think about that last line before you let a proposal use the word agent as decoration. The label is everywhere, but the real thing is rare.

<!--image:2-->

McKinsey's 2025 survey shows the same gap in other numbers. About 88% say they use AI regularly in at least one part of the business, up from 78% a year earlier.[^mckinsey] Only 23% are growing an AI agent system somewhere, and 39% are still trying it out. A consultant who quotes only the first number is describing use and not a finished system. Ask them to say the second pair of numbers out loud. If they cannot, they are selling the feeling of being current.

<!--cta:inline-->

The red flags are easy to spot once you know them. Guaranteed rankings go against Google's own guide. It says the new AI features still depend on ordinary search work.[^google] Nobody can promise a spot in an AI answer. A person who does will probably bluff on the rest of the job too. If there is no data plan, nobody has named the one place the facts live. If there is no handover, your team cannot run the thing after the last invoice. We treat those three as reasons to end the meeting. We do not treat them as issues to talk through.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Sit in on a hiring talk at a small dental clinic. This is a walk-through we use, and it is not a scoreboard. The owner is a dentist who wants help. The office manager runs the reminders and the front desk, and she is in the room because we asked her to be. The bookkeeper is not there yet. She will matter when the invoice arrives, and she should see the proposal before anyone signs.

The first consultant opens a laptop and names a platform. He talks about AI that will "handle the whole patient journey." He has not asked where the appointment book lives. He has not asked about the paper list of people who do not want texts. When the office manager asks who checks a message before it goes out, he says the system has safety rails. A safety rail is not a name. She writes nothing down, and that is the right instinct.

The second consultant does not open a tool. She asks the office manager to describe last Monday, including the part that went wrong. A reminder went to a patient who was already in the chair, because the reminder list and the treatment list do not talk to each other. The consultant writes one sentence. It says to draft cleaning reminders from the appointment record only, and the office manager sends them. She asks where the do-not-contact names are kept. She asks what happens when the manager is out sick. She also says, out loud, that if a ready-made product already drafts that reminder inside the clinic's software, they should buy it and stop talking to her.

We would hire the second person, and we would still make her put a stop rule in the proposal. The work goes on only if the manager can clear the queue in the time she has set aside. It stops if the drafts keep picking the wrong patients. A consultant who will not write the stop rule is planning to stay forever. That is how a small fee turns into the kind of project Gartner expects many AI agent efforts to cancel.

Notice who did the real interview. It was the office manager, and not the owner. The owner felt the pain, but the manager knows the drawer with the paper list. A good consultant talks to the owner about money and risk. Then she talks to the manager about the Monday. A weak one charms the owner and avoids the manager, since the manager asks questions that shrink the proposal. Let it shrink. A smaller job that is true beats a big job that is foggy.

## How we'd run it

We run a hiring talk like a filter. The consultant is not owed a second meeting.

First, we send our questions ahead in writing, so nobody can say they were ambushed. What job will change? Where does the data live? Who checks the answer, by name? How will we know it failed? What will you refuse to build? If the reply is a calendar link and a slide deck with none of those answers, we skip the meeting. Being polite is not a reason to give away an hour.

Second, we hold the meeting with the person who does the work, and not only the owner. We ask the consultant to say the job in one sentence that the staff could repeat. If the sentence has a tool name in it and no verb the staff would use, we send them back. "Roll out the platform" is not a job. "Draft the cleaning reminder and wait for a person" is a job.

Third, we ask the buy-or-build question straight out, and we watch the face. If a ready-made product already does this, will you say so? The honest answer is yes. It comes with a short list of what they could still help with, such as the wording and the checking step. The dishonest answer is a custom build that copies a feature the clinic's software already sells. It pads the consultant's hours and leaves the manager with two systems to look after.

Fourth, we ask for a handover plan before we talk about price. Who can run this when you leave? Where are the rejected drafts written down? What will the bookkeeper see on the invoice, in words and not only in a total? A price with no handover is really a subscription to one person. That can be fine for advice, but it is a bad way to buy a system. The [agency comparison](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) is the page we use when an owner is unsure which kind of help they even want.

Fifth, we check the proposal itself for red flags. Any promise of guaranteed rankings gets a no. Google's guide says the new AI features still depend on ordinary search work. Any slide that quotes use without the gap between use and finished systems gets a question. Any plan that cannot name a risk control gets a no. That is one of the reasons Gartner gave for cancellations. We would rather be called difficult in the first meeting than be stuck in a project that gets canceled after the staff have rebuilt their week around it.

## Common mistakes

The most common mistake is hiring the best talker, and it is a very human one. The owner is busy, and a clear voice feels like skill. In this work, skill sounds slower. It sounds like questions about a drawer full of paper. If you leave a meeting excited and unable to repeat the job in one sentence, you were entertained.

A second mistake is leaving the person who runs the work out of the room. The office manager will inherit the queue. If she first meets the system on launch day, she will find ways around it, and she will be right. Invite her while the proposal can still change. If the consultant objects, that objection tells you what you need to know.

A third mistake is accepting "agent" as a product type, which is how the poll gets ignored. In that Gartner poll of 3,412 people, 19% had made big investments in AI agents, 42% had made small ones, 8% had made none, and 31% were waiting or unsure. Only about 130 vendors met Gartner's bar for a real AI agent product. A proposal that calls a reminder draft an agent is borrowing a word. Ask what the software does on a Monday. If the answer is that it drafts and a person sends, call it a draft. The plainer word will get you a plainer price.

A fourth mistake is the search fantasy, and it can arrive even when you never asked for marketing help. A promise of a top spot in an AI answer tells you the other claims bend too. Google's guide is public. A person who sells certainty against a public guide will sell certainty against your files as well.

The last trap is signing because the quote is small. A small quote with no stop rule has a way of becoming a long one. Cost is one of the reasons these projects get canceled. Get the stop rule in writing while the number still feels harmless.

## What we'd do

We would tell many owners to buy the ready-made product and send the consultant home. That opinion costs us work, and we still hold it. Custom work makes sense when the job depends on your own files and no product will touch them. It also makes sense when the value is the thinking and the handover, and not the code. It does not make sense just because a platform demo was impressive and the office manager was not there to object.

We would also bring the awkward numbers into the proposal review, on purpose. Over 40% of AI agent projects canceled by the end of 2027 is not a reason to avoid all help. It is a reason to ask for a value you can point at and a risk control with a name. The McKinsey gap belongs in the same talk. The consultant will happily say that 88% use AI in at least one part of the business, up from 78% a year earlier. You should be the one to say that 23% are growing an AI agent system and 39% are still trying it out. If they only brought the first number, they are describing a hobby and pricing it like a system.

If the proposal mentions search, rankings, or "being the answer" in an AI result, we stop and open Google's guide with them.[^google] The new AI features still depend on ordinary search work, and no serious person promises the outcome. And if the first test run they show you could not survive a normal week, read the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall) before you pay for a sequel. The [studio](/) will tell you to buy the product when that is the truth. We think you should ask anyone else you pay to say the same thing.

## AI for Small Business: What the Surveys Still Say

The useful question for a small business is which job actually changes. Two surveys from 2025 are still the clean public counts. They do not measure the same thing. One asks whether a small business uses generative AI. The other asks whether a business used AI to make its goods or deliver its service. You can say yes to the first and no to the second, and be honest both times. If you average them into one "how far behind are we" number, you may buy the wrong project.

We wrote out the full split in the [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses). If you want to know what to do about the gap, read the [strategy note](/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business). If you want to score one firm instead of a whole country, use the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment). A survey counts a crowd. Your shop is one set of hands, one set of files, and one job that is slow this week. Start with that job.

People ask us which percentage to believe. We do not treat either one as a verdict on a single owner. What we trust is the wording of the question. If you skip the wording, you can spend a whole season chasing a rank that was never about your counter.

## Two questions, two answers

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] That question is about using a tool to write a product note, draft a reply, or ask for a checklist. It counts the owner who opened the tool on a Tuesday and got something good enough to edit. It does not ask whether a model made the goods on the shelf. It does not ask whether a model did the work the customer paid for.

<!--image:2-->

Statistics Canada found that 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services in 2025, up from 6.1% a year earlier.[^statcan] That question is harder and narrower, because it is about the thing you sell. A bakery that uses a tool to write the weekly email can sit inside the Chamber number and outside the Statistics Canada number. A shop where a model suggests orders and a person places them is close to the second question. It may still not meet it. Read the verbs, which are make and deliver. They are not draft, brainstorm, or "we tried it once."

<!--cta:inline-->

A firm can say yes to the Chamber question and no to the Statistics Canada question. Plan from the job you can name, and do not average the two percentages into one readiness rate. This site does not publish a combined score from the Readiness Check. If someone hands you one blended number made from these two, they have glued different questions together.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk through a home-goods shop with us. This is an example and not a study, and we are not giving it a score. The owner buys from a few makers and from one wholesaler. A floor lead works the counter and knows which lamp has a chip in the glaze. A bookkeeper comes in part of the week and dislikes surprises in her inbox. The shop has no IT person, and the team talks by group text.

Last winter the owner started using a generative tool for product descriptions. She pastes in a few notes from the maker and asks for a short paragraph in her own voice. Then she edits out anything that sounds like a catalog from nowhere. The floor lead does the same for a social post when a new table arrives. He deletes the line that says the wood is oak when it is not. That is real use, so on the Chamber question this shop says yes.

Nothing about that use makes the lamp or delivers the sale. The owner still picks the maker. The floor lead still wraps the lamp and tells the truth about the chip. He also still calls the customer when the freight is late. The bookkeeper still matches each invoice to the packing slip with her own eyes. On the Statistics Canada question, this shop says no. AI is not making the goods, and it is not doing the work for the customer. Both answers are correct. A consultant who says "you are an AI business now" or "you are behind" has not listened.

Here is a job that might move the shop toward the second question, if they ever want that. The wholesaler's invoices arrive as scans, and the bookkeeper retypes every line. A tool could read each scan and suggest the lines while she still posts them herself. That is closer to the back-office service than a nicer lamp description is. It is still not the shop "running on AI." It is one job with one checker, and it touches work they already do to get paid. We would talk about that job for an hour before we ever mentioned the Chamber number.

The trap in this shop is pride that points the wrong way. The owner feels modern because her descriptions got better. Her nephew told her that most small businesses already do this. He was pointing at the Chamber number without saying what the question was. She also feels secretly behind, because a podcast said only a small slice of firms use AI in production. That podcast was pointing at a number like the Statistics Canada one, again without the question. She is not a laggard and she is not finished. She has a drafting habit and an untouched pile of invoices.

## How we'd run it

We do not start by asking an owner where they rank. We start by pulling the two questions apart, and then we pick one job.

First, we ask what they already open in a normal week. The shop owner will name the writing tool. We write that down as use in the Chamber sense. We do not praise it as a plan, and we do not scold it. A product note that a person edits is a fair use of an afternoon. It is not the same as AI doing the work for the customer.

Second, we ask what the customer pays for and what has to be true for the shop to earn it. In this shop the customer pays for the right object, in the shape the floor lead described. It must be handed over or shipped, with books that explain the invoice. We look for any step in that chain where a model already acts. Usually there is none, and we say so. The Statistics Canada answer stays a no. That is useful, because it stops the owner from bragging about a skill she does not have.

Third, we pick one job that could change the chain. We describe it in a sentence a new hire could follow. For this shop we like the scanned invoice better than the caption. The sentence is to read the wholesaler's scan, suggest the lines, and wait for the bookkeeper to post them. If the owner would rather automate the caption, we will do it. But first she must admit that it does not change delivery. That can still be worth a small habit, but it is not worth a project with a name.

Fourth, we name the checker and the failure. The bookkeeper is the checker. A failure is a line that does not match the packing slip, or a vendor she does not know. If she cannot see the original scan next to the suggestion, the job is not safe. We do not turn it on. This is the same care we give any other install, and a survey cannot do it for her.

Fifth, we refuse the blended score. We will not tell this owner that she sits at some midpoint between the two numbers. Those groups and those verbs are different. The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) scores her files, her people, and her job. The [strategy note](/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business) is where the one-page plan goes once the job is chosen. The [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) is the longer story of the split, for the day a partner still wants to argue from a headline.

## Common mistakes

Quoting one percentage in a staff meeting is the fastest way to start a useless argument. When someone says "most small businesses already use it," they are pointing at the Chamber's 58% in 2025. That was up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. A person on the floor hears that they are late. They are not late at wrapping lamps, because they are being compared on a question about generative tools. Say the question out loud or leave the number out.

The mirror mistake is shame from the smaller number. In the Statistics Canada count, 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services in 2025. That was up from 6.1% a year earlier. An owner hears "almost nobody is really doing this" and either freezes or decides the whole topic is hype. Neither reaction picks a job. The smaller number describes a strict question and says nothing about your character.

Averaging the two rates is the mistake we will interrupt every time. A midpoint is not a readiness rate, because the firms, the countries, and the verbs all differ. This site does not publish a combined score from the Readiness Check. We do not want a homemade one in a spreadsheet either. If you want a number for your own business, it has to be about your own business. A national blend cannot tell the bookkeeper whether a scan is readable.

Buying a tool to close the feeling gap is the costly version. The owner sees the gap between "we write notes" and "AI runs the shop." So she buys something that promises to run the shop. Neither survey asked her to do that. The surveys never named her wholesaler, her chipped glaze, or her bookkeeper's part-time days. A purchase that ignores those facts will stall for the usual reasons, and then people will blame the survey.

Treating a yes on the Chamber question as a marketing claim is how trust frays. If a sign in the window says "we use AI" and you only draft captions, a customer will expect something you do not do. We would rather the shop say nothing. The floor lead's honesty about the glaze is worth more than a badge.

## What we'd do

We would plan from the job. We would say the Statistics Canada question out loud before the Chamber one. That is a preference and not a law. Drafting help is legitimate, but it is the easier yes, and it flatters the owner. The question about making goods or doing the service is the one that changes pay, mistakes, and what the customer gets. If the owner only wants drafting help, we will help her keep it small and checked by a person. We will not call it a change in how the shop runs.

We would not tell the home-goods owner that she is behind the 58%. We would not tell her she has "arrived" because she might be inside it either. Arriving means you can name a job on a slow Tuesday and a person checks it. The climb from 23% in 2023 to 40% in 2024 to 58% in 2025 shows chat tool use spreading. The climb from 6.1% to 12.2% in the Statistics Canada numbers shows a stricter habit spreading more quietly. Both can be true, and your shop does not have to pretend to be either crowd.

If a partner brings you a chart this week, ask which question was on the survey. If they cannot say, put the chart down and open the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment). If they can say, and the question is about use and not delivery, read the [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) before you spend money. When you are ready to choose the job, the [strategy note](/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business) is the page we would write with you. We would rather be plain and specific than armed with a number about someone else's work.

## An AI Implementation Framework in Five Stages

An AI implementation framework is the order of work you follow once the job already has a name. NIST calls the risk side of that work Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] We use five stages in plain words, because that is how the talk goes when we sit down with an owner. First we name the job. Then we score the data and write the process. After that we pick a checker, and last we keep the work or stop it.

Most small firms we meet are still in the [Forming band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/band/forming) while those stages are unfinished. A tool is open on someone's laptop and the rest is a hope. A hope is not a stage, and if you skip one you get the stall we describe in the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall). The score that should come before any build is in the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework). This note covers only the order of work after that score exists.

We like a plain, slow order, but most owners like a demo. A demo feels like progress because someone in the room finally relaxes. An order feels like a delay because it is only a list. The list is the work, though, and a framework you cannot walk through on one page is just a brochure. A brochure will not run your business on Monday morning.

## What the numbers say about the middle

McKinsey's 2025 survey says that 88% of people report regular AI use in at least one part of their business.[^mckinsey] That is the easy number, and a seller will quote it before the coffee arrives. The harder numbers sit right beside it. An AI agent is a tool that takes actions on its own. Some 23% of companies are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, while 39% are still trying things out. Among firms that earn less than $100 million, 29% are rolling AI out widely. Among firms that earn more than $5 billion it is nearly half. No more than 10% are rolling out agents in any one part of the business.

If you run a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk, please read that last line slowly. Regular use only means a person opened a tool. Rolling it out in one part of the business means that part runs on a written process, with a person who can stop it. The gap between those two is where projects end up as a browser tab that nobody closes. We do not think a small firm is behind just because it has not rolled out an AI agent system. We think it is right on time if it can finish one job and say honestly who checks the work.

<!--image:2-->

Cisco's 2025 survey of 8,000 leaders found a group called pacesetters, near 13% of that sample. They were 4 times more likely to move a first test run into daily use.[^cisco] Those leaders work in companies with more than 500 employees. A small business can still copy the order the pacesetters followed, which was to write the process first and then put it to work. You cannot copy their staff or their in-house experts. A test run in that survey is also not the same as a receptionist trying a new inbox on a Tuesday. Take the order they followed and leave the rest behind.

<!--cta:inline-->

Stop at the stage you cannot finish. If you cannot name a checker, you are not ready to keep the work. We would rather you pause on a page with a name on it. That beats pushing a half-built flow into a week when the office manager is already behind on the phones.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a neighborhood dental clinic. We use this walk-through when an owner asks what the stages look like in a real week, and it is not a result we measured. The owner is the dentist, and she still does the exams herself. The office manager runs the schedule and answers the billing questions. She also covers the front desk when someone calls in sick. The front-desk lead answers the phone and sends the reminders. A hygienist knows which patients are in the middle of treatment and which ones only need a cleaning.

The job is narrow. Patients who are due for a cleaning get a short reminder that sounds like the clinic. The dentist does not want a computer booking anything clinical or guessing at a balance. She asks for the reminder message and a person who reads it before it goes out.

We write the job in words the front-desk lead can say out loud. The tool drafts the cleaning reminder from the appointment record and never mentions treatment or a price. A person sends it. If a second job is hiding inside that sentence, we start over. A seller will try to make the job wider in the proposal. This one sentence is how we politely say no.

The data gets scored before anyone connects an account. The appointment book lives in the practice software. A paper list in the manager's drawer names people who asked not to be texted. Insurance notes sit on another screen, and the hygienist knows which patients are upset about a bill. Those sources do not agree with each other. A draft built only from the appointment book would write to someone on the paper list. That mistake shows up on the first Monday if anyone looks.

The process is a chain of hands. On Monday morning the front-desk lead pulls the list of patients who are due, and the draft uses the appointment record only. Anything that sounds like a treatment word goes to the hygienist. The office manager reads the rest and sends it. If she is out, the messages wait, because nobody sends one just because the draft sounded sure of itself.

The checker is the office manager, by name, with time held on her calendar. If she cannot do it, the hygienist is the named backup. A checker who is simply whoever happens to be free is not really a checker at all.

After a few real Mondays, they look at what the manager sent back. If the problems are about wording, they keep the job and tighten the line. If the problems are the wrong people, they stop sending and fix the paper list and the appointment book first. Stopping is a finished stage too. The demo took an afternoon, but the paper list and the rule about waiting took the whole month.

## How we'd run it

We run the stages in order, and we do not open the next one while the current one is still a shrug.

First, we sit with the owner and with one person who does the job by hand. We ask to see last week's work on the screen they really use. Then we write one sentence that names the job, the facts it uses, and the thing the tool must not touch. If they want several jobs, we pick the one that happens every week and hurts when it is late. The rest go on a closed list. Opening that list is how a simple reminder turns into the whole patient experience before anyone has sent a real one.

Second, we score the data in the room. We ask where the record lives, who types it, and what happens when it is wrong. We also ask which other list says something different. In the clinic that is the appointment book against the do-not-text drawer. On a trades desk it is the job ticket against the text thread where the customer changed the light fixture. In a shop it is the register against the note scribbled on the bag. If nobody can point at the one place the facts live, we stop. We will not agree to clean it up later, since later is how bad names get a green check.

Third, we write a short script for a loud morning. It says who pulls the list and what the draft may see. It also says who reads it and what to do with a strange one. Last, it says what happens when that person is out. We read it back to the person who will run it. We change it until they say they would follow it on a day when the phones are bad. A script they will not follow is only decoration.

Fourth, we name the checker and hold the time on the calendar before anything is switched on. We also write down where a rejected draft goes, because a side chat does not count. If the rejection stays hidden, the same mistake comes back. Then everyone treats it as brand new.

Fifth, we keep the work or stop it, using a rule we wrote before the first live send. Keep means the checker can clear the queue in the time we held and the rejections are about wording. Stop means we unplug the sending step and go back to the files. We do not add another job to soften the stop. We also do not let a seller rename our sentence as the first step of a big platform.

We stay with the owner through all of this, and not only with the person who bought the license. The owner is the one a friend will text when something goes wrong. So our part is to read the original sentence out loud again whenever people forget it.

## Common mistakes

Starting with the tool is the mistake we see most. A cousin sends a link, and the first hour goes to logins while the job is still a fog. Connecting an account is easy. You cannot quietly undo messages that were sent to people who asked to be left alone.

The demo is the next trap. The records on the screen look clean because someone prepared them, and the do-not-text list is missing. So is the Monday when two people are out. If you sign while the sample is still on the screen, you have bought a performance instead of a tool.

A checker on a slide, and not on a calendar, will let the queue rot. A line like "the office will review it" is not a name. We have watched reminders go out because each person assumed another person had looked. Then the patient heard about a cleaning while already sitting in the chair. The apology lands on the front desk, who never agreed to catch it.

Making a quiet job wider is how a sensible project turns sour. The reminder feels calm, so someone points the same login at billing. A clumsy reminder is an awkward phone call. A wrong balance is a question of trust, and the two do not belong together just because they share a password.

Copying a big-company rollout flatters the room and wears out the desk. Cisco's pacesetters were 4 times more likely to move a first test run into daily use. They also work in companies with more than 500 employees. They have people whose whole job is the process, while you have a manager who also covers lunch. Copy the order they followed, and do not copy a pile of test runs.

Feelings are a mistake of their own, because many owners refuse to stop. A stop feels like a public failure, so a weak flow stays alive. If you stop the sending and put the reason on the same page as the job, the framework worked. A tab that is always being tweaked means it did not.

## What we'd do

We would make the owner pick one job, and we would walk away if she would not. That sounds stern if you wanted a partner who nods along. It is how we have seen this work finish. Use is common, and rolling AI out in one part of the business is rare, since no more than 10% roll out agents in any one part. The firms in that thin slice finished a process. They did not win a contest for the most logins.

We would not aim a clinic at the Cisco pacesetter share. Near 13% of a sample of 8,000 leaders, in companies with more than 500 employees, describes a very different building. The useful part is what they did, which was to write the process first. That let them move a test run into daily use 4 times as often. A clinic can copy that with a manager and a calendar hold. It cannot copy it by wearing out a part-time desk and calling the tiredness progress.

We would keep the old reminder running beside the draft until the manager trusts what she reads. Sellers dislike that, because it makes their product look optional. It still costs less than a week of apologies. When she trusts the draft, we turn the old way off in a sentence the staff can hear. That way nobody keeps doing both in secret.

If a tool is already on your card statement, please do not ask us to make it sound bigger than it is. Ask which stage you cannot finish. A fuzzy job goes back to the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework). A charming demo followed by a bad Monday belongs with the [stall note](/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall). A habit that is still forming can sit in the [Forming band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/band/forming) until the checker has a name. That is a perfectly respectable place to be.

## AI Readiness Assessment Questionnaire: The Themes

An AI readiness questionnaire should bring four themes into the open before anyone names a product. The themes are where the data lives, whether the process is written down, who checks the output, and what a good result would mean. A form that opens with a logo has already skipped the real work.

NIST groups the risk work into four parts, which are Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] We are not asking a small firm to build a risk program with those labels on the door. We are asking the questionnaire to cover the same ground in plain speech. Govern is who gets to decide, and Map is what the job really is. Measure is how you would know the output is wrong. And Manage is what you do when it is. A questionnaire that cannot find those four ideas, even in simpler words, is really a sales form.

The [framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is how we score the answers, and the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is the longer reading. The [growth guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/growth) is what the check offers after the score. Themes come first, and a band comes after that. A tool comes last, and sometimes it does not come at all.

We like a short questionnaire because length feels thorough and often hides the blank. An owner may answer a long run of soft questions and still not say where the record lives. When that happens, the form has dodged the only question that mattered. We would rather ask four blunt questions that are allowed to be answered with "we do not know."

## What a public checklist does not claim
