The AWS checklist for small and midsize businesses, updated in September 2025, walks an owner through readiness questions.[^aws] It does not publish a percentage of businesses that are ready. The OECD SME AI adoption tool, current in 2026, is a self-assessment aid for smaller firms.[^oecd] It is not a national adoption rate.

That missing number is the point of this section, so we will not rush past it. Owners often arrive after reading a headline that sounds like a share of firms. They want their questionnaire to end in the same kind of share. Then they can tell a partner that they are above it or below it. Neither of those public pages will give you that share. AWS gives you questions and a way to talk about stages of work. The OECD tool gives a smaller firm a way to check itself. Suppose your questionnaire prints a readiness rate for "businesses like yours" at the bottom. Then ask who was counted, because if the answer is nobody, you are holding a costume.

We still use those pages, but we use them as prompts and not as a league table. The AWS questions help an owner who has only thought about features. And the OECD aid helps a smaller firm that does not want an account or a stored answer. What you leave with is your own set of answers. You do not leave with permission to say that a percentage of your industry is ready. And we will not write that sentence for you because the sources will not write it either.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Ask where the one place the facts live is for the job. Ask which step is written down and which step is only habit. Ask who can reject the output, and ask what you will stop doing if the answer is weak. Those four questions are the questionnaire.

Say them in the language of the job, or they stay abstract. The question "Where do the facts live?" becomes a plainer one about a real call. When a customer calls about the thing we promised, which page does the person on the phone open? The question about habit becomes a different one. What do we do when the usual person is out, and is that written anywhere a new hire could find? The question about rejecting becomes a third one. Who is allowed to say that this message does not go to the customer? Then the question about what we will stop becomes a last one. If this works, which notebook can we close for good?

A questionnaire that cannot survive that translation is still just a theme list. Themes are not a score, because they are the questions you refuse to skip. We send people to the growth guide once a real score exists. By then the next move is about getting better at the job and not about collecting more questions. Please do not open that guide to avoid the four questions, and open it only after you have answers you can stand behind.

<!--image:3-->

We also want the questionnaire to record disagreement. If the owner and the person who does the job give different answers, the form should show both and not a negotiated average. An average is how a blank turns into a tick. Write "owner says the binder, dispatcher says her head" and leave it ugly. Ugly is honest. A clean tick that needed a compromise in the hallway is how you buy a tool for a process that does not exist.

NIST's four words help us check that we did not drift into product trivia. If the questionnaire never asks who decides, it skipped Govern. And if it never asks what the job is in steps a stranger could follow, it skipped Map. If it never asks how you would notice a wrong output, it skipped Measure. And if it never asks what you will do when the output is wrong, it skipped Manage. You can fail all four tests with a very professional-looking form, and we have watched it happen. The form had sections and a logo but nowhere to write "we do not know."

## A worked example

Say we are at the desk of a small electrical contractor in the late afternoon, when the phones have finally gone quiet. There is an owner, a dispatcher, and a lead who actually walks the jobs. This is an example we walk through, and it is not a firm we audited. We are not going to pretend that we counted their jobs.

The owner was handed a questionnaire by a software seller. It opened with the product name and asked how many users she might want, whether she liked dashboards, and how soon she could start. None of that is a readiness question, so we set it aside and ask our four.

Where do the facts live for a booked job? The owner says the job system. The dispatcher says he keeps a whiteboard because the system is wrong by the time a customer changes a time. The lead says she trusts the text the dispatcher sends her in the morning, because the whiteboard and the system have both let her down. That gives us three answers, and the questionnaire does not get to average them. The one place the facts live is still unresolved, and that unresolved state is the answer we write down.

Which step is written, and which step is habit? The written step is the quote, and the owner is proud of the quote template, as she should be. The habit is everything that happens after the customer says yes. Who tells the lead about the parking note, and who calls the customer when a part slips? Who decides that a job is done enough to invoice? The dispatcher says "we just do it." The lead says she calls the owner when she is unsure, and that means the owner's phone is the process. A step that lives in a phone is not a written step, so we mark it as habit.

Who can reject the output? This is the question that makes the room go quiet, and in a good way. If a tool drafted the morning text to the lead, who could say it is wrong and stop it? The dispatcher assumes he would notice, but the lead says she would notice on site, which is too late. The owner says she would want to approve messages at first. And then she admits she will not read them once the week gets loud. So nobody currently has a real reject button, and the people theme stays blank. We do not fill it in with optimism.

What will they stop doing if the answer is weak? The owner wants to stop repeating the same parking notes, and that is a real stop. The dispatcher wants to stop rebuilding the day from scratch each morning, which is also real. The lead wants to stop arriving without the part. If the questionnaire cannot connect a tool to one of those stops, the tool is only a hobby. So we write the stop next to the blank and let the blank carry a cost they can feel.

We do not end this example with a score, because themes are not a score. The [framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is where those answers get words like absent or partial. And the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is where a band gets explained. What this conversation produced is a form with blanks the owner cannot talk her way out of. That makes it a finished questionnaire, and a finished sale would have been a different meeting and a worse one.

## How we'd run it

First we throw out any question that starts with a product. If a vendor's brochure could answer the sentence, it does not belong on our form. The owner's seller asked about dashboards, but dashboards are a feature. And features are what you discuss after the themes have survived.

Second we ask the four questions in the words of the job, and we pick one job only. At this desk the job is a booked call, from the yes all the way to the lead packing the van. We do not run the questionnaire over the whole company, because a form about "the business" produces slogans. A form about one job produces places, names, and blanks.

Third we ask each person on their own before we let them repair each other's answers. The dispatcher will defer to the owner if she is in the room from the start. And the lead will go quiet if the form starts to sound like a test of her. We want the first answer, which is the one they would give a new hire. Then we put the answers side by side and let the conflict stand.

Fourth we match the answers to Govern, Map, Measure. And Manage without making anyone say those words out loud. Who decides is Govern, and the steps of the booked job are Map. How the lead would know the morning text is wrong is Measure. And what the dispatcher does when it is wrong is Manage. If one of those is missing, the questionnaire is not done, no matter how many other boxes are ticked.

Fifth we decide whether a score is even useful yet. If the facts still live in three different places, a band will only decorate the confusion, so we stay with the questions. If the four themes have answers we can point at, we move to the check and then to the growth guide. That guide is about what to do once you know where you stand, and it is not a way to skip the form.

We keep the session short enough that the lead is not late to a job and the dispatcher is not dispatching from the hallway. A questionnaire filled in by the owner alone on a Sunday night will be complete and also made up. The person who does the step has to be in the room.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is starting with the tool. The seller's form feels efficient because it ends in a quote. But that kind of efficiency is how you skip the record, the habit, and the person who can say no. You will pay for that skip every month.

Another mistake is treating a public checklist as a readiness rate. The AWS page, updated in September 2025, does not publish a percentage of businesses that are ready. And the OECD aid, current in 2026, is not a national adoption rate. If your notes say "we are ahead of most firms," then you wrote a sentence your sources refused to write.

A third mistake is smoothing over disagreement. When the owner, the dispatcher, and the lead name different records, the honest questionnaire shows the split. A single tick marked "system of record: yes" is a fiction they agreed to so the meeting could end. Ending the meeting is not the goal. The blank is the goal.

We also see forms that ask about attitude, and "How excited is your team about AI?" is not a theme. Excitement does not tell you where the facts live. A doubtful lead who can reject a bad text is more ready than a cheerful room with no reject button. So we ask about permission and not about mood.

The last mistake is a questionnaire with no "stop doing" line. If nothing will be stopped, then nothing was decided, and you only gathered opinions. You did not assess the job.

## What we'd do

We would use a one-page form with those four questions and a place to write two names when the answers conflict. Our opinion is that a long assessment questionnaire is often a way to feel serious without naming the whiteboard. The owner does not need more questions. She does need the dispatcher's answer and the lead's answer on the same sheet, in ink, where a dashboard question used to be.

If we were sitting with them next week, we would not bring a tool. We would bring the four questions again and see whether the facts now live in one place. If they do, we would score it, and if they do not, we would still not buy. A questionnaire that cannot produce a no is not an assessment, because it is only a path to a signature.

## AI Readiness Assessment: What It Measures and How to Score

An AI readiness assessment asks whether a business can put a new tool to work. Public indexes and checklists answer that question for different groups of people. The groups are easy to mix up. This note compares them. Then it explains what the [Readiness Check guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) scores for the firm that is actually in the room.

We get asked for "our number," as if readiness were a credit score you could borrow from a headline. A figure about leaders at big companies cannot tell a clinic whether the front desk and the clinician use the same record.

## What the public tools measure

Cisco put out its third yearly AI Readiness Index on 14 October 2025. It surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at companies with more than 500 employees. Those leaders came from 30 markets and 26 industries.[^cisco] The leaders it calls pacesetters stayed near 13% of the sample for three years. Those companies were 4 times more likely to turn a first trial into real use. They were also 50% more likely to see real value. Of all the people surveyed, 83% plan to use AI agents. Nearly 40% expect agents to work beside staff within a year. That sample is not a small-business survey.

Owners hear the Cisco line on a podcast and wonder if they are behind. Behind what, and compared with whom? They would be behind a company big enough to put a senior leader on a survey. The 13% figure is a fair check for large firms. It is a poor mirror for a practice with a front desk and two treatment rooms.

One part still fits a small firm, and that is the gap between a trial and daily work. The companies that cross that gap have the job written down. The demo was never the hard part. So if you use Cisco at all in a small firm, use it as a warning against mistaking a trial for a habit. Please do not use it as a ranking that you are supposed to join.

Gartner said on 26 February 2025 that 63% of the people it asked do not have the data habits that AI needs. Some of them were also not sure they had those habits.[^gartner] The same note predicts that through 2026, companies will give up on 60% of AI projects that lack data made ready for AI. We point to that line when someone wants to skip the record and start with a login. The project stops when the data was never ready. That story is not hard to guess.

The OECD tool for small and midsize firms is a short self-check about AI use. It is part of the work of the 2026 French Group of Seven Presidency.[^oecd] It takes about five minutes and stores no data. Your answers stay in the browser. As of May 2026 it is a test version, and Group of Seven governments are still checking it. It does not publish an adoption rate. We like it as a set of questions you can answer without making an account. We do not like it as a stand-in for a national share, because it never claims to be one.

AWS posted an AI readiness checklist in September 2025.[^aws] It walks through five steps and sorts a business into four stages. The stages run from Not yet ready, through Emerging and Operational, to a last stage about using AI widely. They cover the data, the use case, the tools, the rules, and the numbers you will watch. The page does not cite an adoption percentage. Stages are plain descriptions that you can argue with. A percentage that nobody counted is just a rumor with a percent sign.

<!--image:2-->

Here is a plain comparison of who each tool describes and what you leave with.

- Cisco's index describes companies with more than 500 employees, so you get a comparison with pacesetters and not a score for one small firm.
- The OECD tool describes the smaller firms in the Group of Seven test, so you get a short self-check that stays in the browser.
- The AWS checklist describes a small or midsize business, so you get five steps and four stage names.
- The Readiness Check describes the business taking it, so you get four scores, a band, and three tips for each section.

The Readiness Check is the one built for the firm in the room. It teaches and points the way, but it does not diagnose. We publish the method on [our site](/).

We draw that line on purpose. A diagnosis says what is wrong with you. A route says where to look next. Owners sometimes want the diagnosis because it sounds more serious, but serious is not the same as useful. If we told a clinic that it had failed readiness, we would be borrowing a doctor's tone for a business talk. The check describes where you stand and points to a next page. That is the promise we make.

<!--cta:inline-->

## What each band means

The check scores from 0 to 100. The bands are Early (0–39), Forming (40–59), Ready (60–79), and Running (80–100).[^check]

- Early: The work that matters still lives in people's heads, so the first useful step is to write one job down and name who owns it.
- Forming: Parts of the work are written down, so a named owner and one place for the facts can turn that into something a team can run.
- Ready: The business can put a new tool to work, so the open question is which job to start with and who owns it day to day.
- Running: A real job already uses the tools, so the next gain is the job that still waits on one person.

<!--image:3-->

A band tells you where you stand today. It is not a grade. The four scores behind it are data, process, people, and the decision. The check takes five to seven minutes with one question on each screen. It gives three tips for each section.

Early means the know-how is still in people's heads. So you write one job down and name the owner before you shop. Forming means the writing is only partial. Two pieces are missing. One is a named owner, and the other is one place where the facts live. Without them nobody else can run the job when the usual person is out.

Ready means a new tool can land. The argument left is which job goes first and who lives with it on an ordinary day. Running means a real job already uses the tools. The gain left is the job that still waits on one person. Everyone goes around that job because it is "easier to ask her."

People treat Running as the compliment and Early as the scolding, but we do not. Early is a clear description, and it is often the honest one. A clinic can be excellent at care and still be Early at the paperwork around recalls. Those are different skills. The band is about whether a tool has anything solid to stand on. It is not a review of the owner's character.

The next note looks at [how surveys count AI in small businesses](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses). That is a different question from whether one firm is ready. A survey can talk about firms in general. It cannot say whether your front desk and your clinician agree on the chart note. We try not to let the wide question answer the narrow one.

## A worked example

Say we are in a small physiotherapy clinic after the last patient has gone home. One person runs the front desk. One clinician sees most of the repeat visits. This is an example we walk through, and it is not a clinic we measured.

The owner has been shown a tool that would draft recall messages and sum up visit notes. She wants to know if the practice is "ready" before she signs. We do not start with the tool. We start with the four scores, in plain words, the way the check will later turn them into a band.

Data for the recall job is a mess in the ordinary sense. The front desk lead has a list in the booking screen. The clinician keeps a notebook of people he meant to see again. The owner trusts a spreadsheet she built when the booking screen lost a column. Asked which list is right, they look at each other. That is not a failure of care. But it does mean there is no one place where the facts live. We would not call the data "in place" while three lists can disagree and nobody minds.

Process is only partial. The easy path is spoken aloud. The clinician finishes, the front desk lead books the next visit, and the patient leaves with a card. The odd cases are never spoken at all. What if the patient will not book today? What if the clinician wants a recall in six weeks, but the front desk lead only sees open slots this month? What if the note is not done before the patient reaches the desk? The owner says they "work it out." That is Forming at best, because a tool cannot follow it without making up the rest.

People are the surprise, as in most rooms. The front desk lead already pastes awkward wording into a personal chat tool so the recall text sounds less cold. The clinician did not know, and neither did the owner. Nobody has said whether those words may go to a patient. The people score is not about how eager everyone is. It is really about who has permission to do what.

The decision is still a blank. The owner says success would be "fewer no-shows." But she cannot say who would turn the tool off if a message went to the wrong person. Until that answer exists, we will not talk about agents, trials, or pacesetters. Cisco's picture of large firms is interesting. It has nothing to say about whether the front desk lead and the clinician share a list.

If we scored this room in the check's language, we would expect Early or Forming. We would say so plainly. The work that matters for this job still lives in heads and side lists. The useful step is to write the recall job down and name who owns it. That is just what the Early line says.

## How we'd run it

First, we name one job, and at the clinic it is the recall. It runs from the clinician deciding someone should come back to the patient actually having a time. If the owner says "everything," we shrink it until it has a clear start and a clear finish.

Second, we pull the public tools apart so nobody borrows the wrong group of people. Cisco describes companies with more than 500 employees. The OECD tool is a short self-check that publishes no rate. AWS offers stage names without an adoption percentage. None of those is a score for this clinic, and we say so before anyone feels behind.

Third, we score data, process, people, and the decision in words. We use absent, partial, in place, or running. We use the last two only if we can point to proof. The front desk lead, the clinician, and the owner each answer on their own. When they disagree, that is the finding. So we write it down and do not average it into a mood.

Fourth, we take the check if they want the band. It takes five to seven minutes, with one question on each screen and three tips for each section. We read Early, Forming, Ready, or Running as a place to stand today. We do not add a pep talk that turns Early into "almost Ready."

Fifth, we pick one next page and not five projects. If the record is the blank, we fix the list that the front desk lead and the clinician will both believe. If the writing is the blank, we write down what happens for the patient who will not book today. The tool demo can wait until that page exists.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is treating Cisco's pacesetters as a small-business grade. Near 13% of a large-firm sample were 4 times as likely to turn a first trial into real use. That is a fact about those firms. Quoting it at a clinic as "only the top shops are ready" makes up a ranking that the study never made.

Another mistake is averaging the four scores into a feeling. Data can be absent while people are eager, and eagerness is not a score. The band names where you stand. The useful part is the weak spot, and not the average comfort in the room.

A third mistake is reading the OECD tool's silence as a zero. It does not publish an adoption rate, but that does not show that small firms are unready. It shows a tool that refused to pretend.

We also watch owners jump from a band to a purchase in the same sitting. Ready still asks which job to start with and who owns it day to day. The band did not pick the vendor, so you still have to.

## What we'd do

We would score the clinic in front of us and leave Cisco in the footnote where it belongs. In our view a small practice does not need to know whether it is a pacesetter. It needs to know whether the front desk lead's list and the clinician's notebook are the same list. Until they are, a recall tool will write confident messages from a record nobody owns.

If we were the owner, we would spend the next few ordinary weeks on one written recall path. It would include the patient who will not book at the desk. We would also ask the front desk lead to stop sending patient wording from a personal account until the owner has said what may go out. Then we would take the check again and read the band as a place to stand and not a prize. If it still says Early, we would believe it.

## AI Readiness Checklist Before You Buy a Tool

An AI readiness checklist is the list of questions you answer before you pay for a tool. We use it when an owner has a demo booked. The owner has not yet said which job the tool is for. The questions fall into four groups, which are data, process, people, and the decision. A vendor's feature list cannot stand in for any of them.

The [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) scores the same four groups. The [assessment note](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) compares the public tools, and the [data note](/blog/ai-ready-data) stays on the first group. If the process score is your weak spot, the [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-low) is the page we hand over.

We think of the checklist as a brake. The tour of a tool always looks tidy. The real test comes on the busy afternoon after it, when nobody remembers which screen is the right one. A tick means you can point to the answer, and a blank means you cannot. The blanks are the useful part.

## Data and process

Here are the questions for the first two groups. Can you name the one place the facts live for this job? Is it current, and can a system read it without someone retyping it? Is the job written down, including the exceptions, and does one person own the handoff?

We ask these out loud. The person who does the work must be in the room, and not only the person who signs the check. The owner answers from memory, and the person at the counter answers from last Thursday. When the two disagree, the list has already paid for itself.

Every shop we sit in has more than one place where a fact can live. There is the notebook, the spreadsheet the bookkeeper trusts, the supplier portal, and the text thread. The record you mean is whichever one the next person will believe when they disagree. If you cannot name that one, a new tool just becomes another place to hunt.

Next we ask whether the record is current and whether a system can read it. A record that gets patched from memory is more of a souvenir than a source. For an open order, current means the status changed when the part came in. It does not mean someone updated it after they remembered to call. If someone still has to retype the record, the tool will wait on that person. Retyping is the job you have not replaced yet.

The process questions sit beside the data questions because a clean record with no written handoff will still stall. We want the happy path and the exceptions too. What happens when the part is wrong? What if the customer does not answer, or the usual person is out? If those live only as habit, the tool will follow the happy path and make up the rest. One person has to own the handoff, even on the day that person is out. A handoff that everyone owns tends to belong to no one.

In February 2025, Gartner reported that 63% of respondents do not have the data practices that AI needs, or are not sure they do.[^gartner-data] The same note says that through 2026 companies will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. We read that as a reason to treat the data questions as the main event. A large firm and a small counter can fail the same way. The record is not ready, and the project dies once the demo fades.

AWS published a checklist in September 2025.[^aws] It walks through five steps. It sorts a business into four stages, called Not yet ready, Emerging, Operational, and Scaling. The page does not cite an adoption percentage, and we like that. A stage name is a description you can argue with. If a page will not say how many firms it counted, do not turn its silence into a rate.

We use those stage names as labels and not as a grade. Not yet ready means the job still lives in one person's head. Emerging means some of it is written down while a lot of it is habit. Operational means your staff can run the job without a hero. Scaling means you repeat a pattern instead of finding it. You do not have to adopt the labels, but you do have to say which one fits.

<!--image:2-->

We open the process guide when this half of the list is mostly blank. We fix the writing before we fix the software. A short written handoff, with the exceptions on the same page, beats a tool that thinks the handoff is already there.

## People and the decision

Who may use a tool, and who may send its output to a customer? Those are the people questions, and they are where checklists tend to go soft. "Everyone will use it" is not an answer. A name is an answer, and so is a rule about what can leave the building.

Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work. It says 46% of those users started less than six months earlier.[^microsoft] It also says 78% of AI users bring their own tools, and at small and midsize companies that share is 80%. It also says 60% of leaders worry that their company's leadership lacks a plan and vision to put AI in place.

In a small company those figures show up as one person. Someone is already pasting notes into a personal account because the official way is slow. They are only trying to finish the day. A checklist that never asks who brought a tool in will miss the real system. That system is often the one in a coat pocket.

We ask who uses the tool on a normal day. We ask who may send its words to a customer. We also ask who can stop it when it is wrong. If nobody can stop it, you do not have a people plan. You have a hope that the errors will be obvious.

The decision questions are separate. What would count as success, who can stop the experiment, and what happens if the tool is wrong? "Sam will keep an eye on it" names a person. "The customer hears from the record, not from memory" is a decision. So is "if it sends a wrong message, we turn it off the same day." We write each one on its own line.

<!--cta:inline-->

A tick list does not tell you which gap is largest. The Readiness Check turns the same four groups into a band. We still want the paper list first. A band without a talk is just a costume on a number. The list is the talk. The band is what you get when you want the same questions scored the same way next time.

<!--image:3-->

When the room is being polite, we add one more decision question. What will you stop doing if this works? If the answer is nothing, the tool is a hobby. The checklist is allowed to end with a no. A no that names the blank box is a better result than a yes that names a logo.

## A worked example

Say we are sitting after close with the owner of a neighborhood hardware shop. A counter lead and a bookkeeper are there too. This is an example we walk through, and it is not a report of a shop we measured.

The owner wants a tool that drafts the message saying a special order is in. It would also suggest which supplier to chase. The demo was slick, but the checklist is the part where we ignore the demo.

We start with data. The owner says the computer is the one place the facts live. The counter lead keeps a notebook because the computer is wrong whenever a quantity changes at the counter. The bookkeeper trusts a spreadsheet she updates from supplier emails. She has to pay someone, and the other two records disagree. So the box for one place the facts live stays blank. We ask which record he would trust if the owner were out, and the counter lead says the notebook. Then he says he would call the bookkeeper. That makes a person the record. A person can be a bridge, but a tool cannot read a person.

Then comes the process. A part arrives, someone calls, the customer picks up, and the bookkeeper marks it paid. That is the easy happy path. A damaged part goes on the back shelf until the counter lead deals with it. A customer who does not answer gets one more try, and then the order just sits. None of that is written down. On days when the counter lead is at the other site, the handoff has no owner. We refuse to count the happy path as the whole process.

Then people. The counter lead already uses a chat tool on his phone to reword messages. He does it when he is tired of sounding stiff, and the owner did not know. We do not scold him. Instead we write down the question the checklist was made for. Who may send those words to a customer, and who may not?

Then the decision. The owner says success is less chaos, so we push once. Success is that a customer hears about an arrival from the record, and not from the counter lead's memory. The bookkeeper should also see the same status the counter lead sees. If a message goes out wrong, the owner can stop the trial herself without waiting for a vendor. That line is what lets her buy later without betting the shop on a login.

We leave with blanks on data and process and a surprise on people. The decision is finally a sentence. Nobody bought anything, and that is the checklist working.

## How we'd run it

We run it as a short working session and not as homework we email into the void.

First, we pick one job, and not the whole business. We want one job with a start and a finish. In the shop that job is the special order. It runs from the promise to the moment the customer has the part or hears that it failed. If you pick every job, you will not tick anything honestly.

Second, we put the people who touch that job in the room. The owner alone will describe the job she wishes existed. The counter lead will describe the job that exists, and the bookkeeper will describe the job that gets paid. All three answers belong on the sheet.

Third, we walk through data, then process, then people, then the decision, and we write the blanks in ink. We do not shop for tools in the middle. If someone says the new software would handle that, we write "not handled today" and keep going.

Fourth, we read the blanks back and name one owner for the next change. If the missing record is the blank that matters, the two of them agree on what they will treat as the record on ordinary days. The owner's job is to back that choice when it is inconvenient.

Fifth, and only then, we look at tools with the sheet on the table. Any feature that does not touch a ticked box or a named blank is a distraction. If the blanks are still the whole story, we stop. A process blank goes to the process guide. The same four groups go to the check when we want a band instead of ticks.

We book the session after the rush. We keep it short so the counter lead is not watching the door. A checklist filled in by the owner alone at midnight will be full, but it will be wrong.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is ticking the box you hope is true. "We have a process" often means a binder from a quieter year. If the counter lead cannot find the page for a damaged part, you do not have a process for the job you are buying for.

Another mistake is letting the vendor's questionnaire replace yours. Their questions ask whether you can be a customer. Yours ask whether the job can survive contact with a tool. Keep yours, even if yours is a notebook page.

A third mistake is calling a shared inbox a system of record. An inbox is a pile that happens to be searchable, and it is current only if someone sorted it. The checklist asks whether a system can read the record without a person retyping it. A pile fails that test.

We also watch owners score their own confidence and write down only the happy path. Confidence is a mood, but the checklist is a pointing exercise. The exceptions are the list.

## What we'd do

We would not buy in the meeting where the checklist is first filled in. We would buy later, for one job. First the one place the facts live needs a name, and the handoff needs a person. Our view is simple. A tool on top of three records will just make another record. You will pay a fee and still call the bookkeeper.

If we were the owner, we would spend the next few ordinary days on one thing. The counter lead and the bookkeeper would write status in one place, including the damaged-part case. We would also pause the counter lead's phone tool for customer messages. It stays paused until the owner says what may be sent. That is a smaller project than a new platform. It is also the project the checklist was trying to start.

We would treat a full page of ticks with suspicion and a short page of blanks with respect. The blanks are the work, and the tool can wait.

## An AI Readiness Framework an Owner Can Score

An AI readiness framework is a way to score the business before you score a tool. We use it when an owner wants a plan and all anyone has offered is a product tour. The tour can wait, because the score is about the work.

NIST groups AI risk work as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] This note uses four groups an owner can see, which are data, process, people, and the decision. We call each group absent, partial, in place, or running. Those words are anchors and not a percentage. If you cannot point at the thing, you do not get the stronger word. We would rather call data absent than call it running because the owner feels modern.

The [readiness guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) is the matching page. The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is the longer note, and the [questionnaire](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment-questionnaire) is the list of questions. The framework is what you do with the answers once they are on paper. You do not turn them into a fake share of readiness. You give each group a word you can defend.

## What the bands mean

The Readiness Check scores 0 to 39 as Early, 40 to 59 as Forming, 60 to 79 as Ready, and 80 to 100 as Running.[^check] The check helps you see where to look next. It does not certify a business.

Read those bands as a shape and not as a medal. Early means the work that matters still lives in people's heads. Forming means some of it is written down, but nobody clearly owns it. Ready means you could put a system on the job without making up the job at the same time. Running means the tools already do real work, and the leftover pain is the task everyone still hands to one person. A band without those sentences is just a number. We do not certify anyone with it, because certifying is what a buyer wants to wave at a board. A small firm has no such board, and we will not pretend the check is a seal.

<!--image:2-->

Gartner said in February 2025 that 63% of respondents do not have, or are unsure they have, the data practices AI needs.[^gartner-data] Through 2026, companies will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. A framework that scores data as running while the facts sit in a shared inbox is scoring a wish. We keep that idea in the room during the talk. The research is about the people Gartner asked and not about your shop. It still describes the failure we watch, where the project looks alive until the record has to carry it.

Cisco's 2025 index surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at companies with more than 500 employees.[^cisco] The leaders it called pacesetters were near 13%, and their companies were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production. That group is not a small business. The pattern still matters, because production follows a written process and not a demo. If you quote the 13% at a bakery and call the baker not a pacesetter, you have changed the group. The framework helps us avoid that slide. We score the bakery in words, and we do not borrow a big-company league table.

<!--cta:inline-->

Score the four groups in words first. Then run the check if you want the band. Words come before numbers because a number is easy to flatter. If you jump to the band, you will argue with the number and not with the inbox.

<!--image:3-->

Here is how we pick the words, so they do not turn into moods. Data is absent when nobody can name the record. It is partial when a record exists, but people keep a side copy they trust more. It is in place when one current record is the one a new person would open, and a system could read it without anyone retyping it. It is running when that record already feeds a job you do every week, and someone notices when a field is wrong.

Process is absent when the steps live in one person's head. It is partial when the usual path is written down and the exceptions are folklore. It is in place when the exceptions sit on the same page and one person owns the handoff, even on the day they are out. It is running when everyone follows that page without a meeting to find it again.

People is absent when nobody has said who may send output to a customer, and nobody has noticed that someone already does. It is partial when use is casual and nobody knows who can say no. It is in place when a named person may use the tool, a named person may send, and a named person may stop it. It is running when that stop has been used at least once and not just promised.

The decision is absent when success means less chaos. It is partial when success has a name but nobody can end the trial. It is in place when success, the person who can stop it, and the rule for wrong output are all written as sentences. It is running when you have already stopped something because the rule said to. A decision that has never met a bad week is still a draft.

The band sits on top of those words and does not replace them. Early, Forming, Ready, and Running tell you the shape, and the four words tell you where to work. We have watched owners cheer for Ready and ignore a data score that was still partial. The framework makes that cheer walk past the weak group first.

## A worked example

Say we are in a small bakery after the morning rush. One person runs the front, and another runs the kitchen and the special-order book. This is an example we walk through, and it is not an audit. We did not measure their flour, and we will not invent a before and after.

The owner wants a tool that answers catering emails and suggests a quote. The demo replied faster than the front lead can. The framework is the part where we ignore the speed and score the job.

First, data. The special-order book is a paper notebook in the kitchen. The front lead also keeps notes in the shop inbox, because customers write to the shop address. The owner has a price sheet that is mostly current. We ask which record a quote must match, and the three of them do not agree. So data is absent for the catering job, even though a notebook exists. A notebook that nobody treats as final is not the one place the facts live. Calling it in place because paper feels solid would be the wish Gartner warns about, where the project is dropped later because the data was never ready. We say absent.

Next, process. The usual path is real. An email comes in, the kitchen lead checks the book, the owner sets a price, and the front lead replies. The exception is a customer who changes the head count the day before, or a date the kitchen lead half promised on the phone. Nobody wrote that down, so process is partial. The usual path is not the whole process. If we scored it in place, the tool would invent the head count change and sound sure about it.

Then people. The front lead already drafts replies in a personal account when she falls behind, and then she pastes them into the inbox. The owner did not know that customer words were being drafted somewhere else. Nobody is named as the person who may send, and nobody is named as the person who may block a send. People is partial, and it leans toward absent on the permission that matters. We do not call it good enough just because the front lead is capable. Capable is not the same as allowed.

Last, the decision. The owner says success is more catering without more evenings. That is almost a sentence. He cannot say what would make him turn the tool off, except if it felt wrong. A feeling is not a rule, so the decision is partial. We will not average these four words into a cheerful Ready. Absent data and partial everything else is an Early or Forming shape. We would rather say that than borrow the pacesetter story for a bakery that was not in the sample.

We leave the owner with four words and one job, and not with a percentage or a certificate. The next move is to pick one record, either the notebook or the inbox, and make it the one that counts. Then write down the head count exception, and name who may send. After that, a band means something.

## How we'd run it

First, we pick the job the tool is meant to touch. At the bakery it is the catering reply, from the first email to a price the kitchen can keep. If the owner says the framework should cover the whole shop, we narrow it. A framework about everything scores nothing.

Second, we put the front lead and the kitchen lead in the room, and not only the owner. The owner describes the price list. The front describes the inbox, and the kitchen describes the book. The framework is a pointing exercise, and people who do not touch the job cannot point.

Third, we give data, then process, then people, then the decision one of the four words. We say each word out loud and wait to see if anyone objects. An objection usually means we were about to flatter the group. We move a word down when we cannot point at the proof. We never move it up because the demo was good.

Fourth, we look at the check only then, if they want the band from 0 to 100. The band has to fit the four words. If data is absent, a low band should not surprise anyone, and we should not argue it upward to protect the owner's mood.

Fifth, we choose one group to move up a single step. Absent data becomes partial when one record gets a name, and not when a tool arrives. Partial process becomes in place when the head count exception sits on the same page as the usual path. We do not try to move all four groups in one panicked week. We take one step with one owner, and then we look again.

Sixth, we keep Cisco and Gartner in their proper jobs. They explain why data and production matter. They do not grade the bakery. If someone in the room quotes a big-company index as the owner's score, we put the framework sheet back in the middle of the table.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is using the strong word because it sounds like progress. Calling a shared inbox running is the mistake we named above, and it is common because the inbox is busy. Busy is not the same as a record a system can read. A busy inbox is just a pile with a pulse.

Another mistake is scoring the owner's hopes and not the job. The owner wants catering to grow, but hope is not one of the four groups. The groups are data, process, people, and the decision. If those are weak, the hope is a wish with a login.

A third mistake is bringing a pacesetter comparison into a small firm. Cisco's 2025 index covers senior leaders at companies with more than 500 employees. The pacesetters near 13%, and the 4 times better odds of moving a pilot into production, describe that group. The bakery is not in it. We keep the pattern, which is a written process, and we drop the ranking.

We also see people skip the decision because it feels soft. It is the group that keeps a trial from turning into a plan you are afraid to cancel. If nobody can stop the experiment, you do not have a framework. You have a purchase.

## What we'd do

We would score in words and stay there until the words stop embarrassing us. In our view the band is a convenience and the four words are the work. A bakery that can say data is absent, and the kitchen lead's notebook is what we will make true, is ahead of a bakery that can quote a readiness percentage it did not earn.

If we were the owner, we would stop answering catering emails from side drafts until the inbox and the book agree on which one wins. We would also write the head count change on the same card as the quote steps. Then we would take the check. If the band says Early, we would believe it and keep going, because the framework did its job when it stopped a fast yes.

## AI-Ready Data: What a Small Business Needs First

AI-ready data for a small business is one current place a system can read. It also needs a person who knows which fields are wrong. It is not a warehouse, a lake, or a platform with a serious name. If the answer lives only in someone's head, the tool will make up a second version. That version will sound very sure of itself.

Owners often hear that they must "get their data ready," as if that meant hiring consultants. It sounds like you must also buy a new place to store everything. For the job in front of you, ready means something much smaller. You need one place for the facts. It has to be current enough that the person doing the job trusts it today. A system has to be able to read it without anyone retyping it. And someone has to know which fields look fine but are not. If you cannot point at that place, stop the purchase.

The [low-data guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-data-low) and the [mid-data guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-data-mid) are the matching fixes. The [checklist](/blog/ai-readiness-checklist) asks the same question before you buy anything. Low means you cannot yet name the place the facts live. Mid means you have something, but a system should not trust it yet. Neither guide is a shopping list.

## What the research counts

Gartner reported in February 2025 that 63% of respondents lack the data management practices AI needs, or are unsure they have them.[^gartner-data] It also said that through 2026, firms will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. We do not cite the sample size here, because the article and its structured data do not agree on it.

We keep that last point because it is easy to turn a percentage into more precision than it has. The 63% is what the note reports about the people it asked. We will not add a sample size that the page does not let us stand behind. The useful part is the shape of the failure. Firms go ahead without the practices, and then they drop the projects. A tool can be full of features and still be unsupported if the record under it is a guess.

A later Gartner article is from January 2026. It says at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after the first test run by the end of last year.[^gartner-fail] The reasons it gives are poor data quality, weak risk controls, rising costs, and unclear business value.

Read those reasons as ways a first test run can flatter you. The demo works on a clean slice that someone prepared by hand. Poor data quality shows up when the real record arrives, with blank fields and two spellings of the same customer. Weak risk controls show up when nobody is allowed to stop a wrong answer. Rising costs show up when the retyping you hoped to delete is still there. Now there is a new fee too. Unclear value shows up when you cannot say what you stopped doing. The figure for abandoned projects describes work that looked like a success once. So it is a good reason to refuse a test that uses better data than you really have.

<!--image:2-->

| Where the knowledge lives | What a tool can do with it |
| --- | --- |
| Only in one person's head | Almost nothing that can be repeated |
| In documents that no system can read | A person still has to retype it all |
| In one system with a current record | The job can be tried |

<!--cta:inline-->

Pick one job and name the place its facts live. If you cannot, stop the purchase and fix that first. That is the whole data test.

The table is the test, and owners often answer it with a tour of their software instead of a location. If the knowledge lives in one person's head, a tool has almost nothing it can repeat. If it lives in documents no system can read, a person still retypes, which means you bought a second job. If it lives in one system with a current record, the job can be tried. Tried is the honest word, because the table does not promise success. It only says the attempt is no longer make-believe.

We add one more question in conversation that the table does not need to print. It is who knows which fields are wrong. A current record can still flatter you. The phone number may be right while the box that says "approved for the extra work" is only wishful. The person who knows that is part of AI-ready data. A warehouse without that person is just a larger place to be wrong.

<!--image:3-->

There are two phrases we will not accept in place of a named place for the facts. "We have a lot of data" means a pile, and a pile is not kept current on purpose. "We can export it" means a person can make a snapshot that starts going stale while the file downloads. An export is a document. If no system can read the live record, you are in the middle row of the table. The person who exports it has become the process. Fix the place they export from before you call the export a plan.

## A worked example

Say we are in the office of a small landscaping company on a weekday morning. One person does the scheduling and another leads a crew. This is an example we walk through, so we are not reporting their routes or their revenue. There is no measured before and after, only a job and a question about where its record lives.

The job the owner wants a tool to do is the customer update. It says what the crew did, what is left, and whether the customer owes a decision about extra work. A vendor showed a draft that sounded like the crew lead, only smoother. The owner liked the sound, so we asked where the facts in that draft would come from.

The scheduler says the booking tool is the answer, because it knows the address and the time window. The crew lead says the truth is in the note she writes in a group text. She sends it after the crew walks the yard. The owner keeps a spreadsheet of who has approved extras. He does not trust the booking tool with money questions. That makes three homes for one update. A draft built from the booking tool alone will miss the yard note and may invent the approval. The made-up version will sound like the crew lead. It will be wrong in the way that costs trust.

Using the words of the table, the knowledge lives partly in one person's head until she sends her text. That head is the crew lead's. It also lives in documents the booking tool does not read, which are the group text and the owner's spreadsheet. It does not yet live in one system with a current record of the whole job. A system could read the address. It could not read "the side bed was wetter than expected, so we stopped and need a yes on the extra drainage." That only works if someone retypes it into a field. So the middle row is the honest row, because a person still has to retype. Buying the draft tool now adds a voice to the retyping and does not remove it.

We then ask who knows which fields are wrong. The crew lead knows the yard, and the scheduler knows which customers answer their phones. The owner knows his spreadsheet falls behind whenever he is out on a job himself. The record is split across a text, a schedule, and a sheet, and current means something different in each one. For the customer update, current has to mean this morning's yard plus whether the extra work is approved. They do not have one place that holds both.

What we would not do is start a first test run on last month's cleanest jobs. If the test only runs on yards the scheduler already tidied, it is a performance and not a test. A real test uses a messy yard that the crew lead has not typed up yet. That is how a flattering demo ends up among the projects abandoned after the first test run.

The fix is dull, which is why it works. We pick the customer update as the only job. Then we pick one place where the yard note and the approval must both land before a message goes out. The crew lead's text can stay a scratch pad. She or the scheduler just has to move the real sentence into that place the same day. The owner's spreadsheet can stay his private worry list until the approval is also in the shared record. Then a tool can be tried, because there is one current place for the facts. Until then, the low-data guide is the right page to read, and the vendor's order form is not.

## How we'd run it

First we name the job in one sentence. We do not say "our data." We say the customer update, or the open order, or the recall. If the sentence needs a list of every service you sell, we have not named a job yet. Data readiness without a job is a storage talk. Storage is how you end up buying a warehouse you do not need.

Second we ask each person where they would look if the owner could not be reached. The scheduler's answer, the crew lead's answer, and the owner's answer all go on one sheet. If the answers match, we still ask whether a system can read that place or whether someone retypes it. If the answers do not match, the place is not named yet. We stop pretending the booking tool won just because it has a logo.

Third we mark the table's row in ink. The row is one person's head, documents no system can read, or one system with a current record. We do not invent a fourth row called "we are getting there." Getting there is the middle row plus a plan. The plan is a person and a place, and not a purchase.

Fourth we name who knows which fields are wrong, and we write the fields down. For the crew, the wrong field is often an approval given out loud on site. It never reached the owner's sheet. That field does not go into a customer message until it is in the shared record. This is the risk-control reason from the later Gartner article in small form. Somebody can say the output is not allowed to include a guess.

Fifth we decide low or mid before we decide tool or no tool. If we cannot name the place, we are in the low-data guide and the purchase stops. If we can name it but a person still retypes the part the tool would need, we are in the mid-data guide. The work is to make that part readable. Only the bottom row of the table gets a trial. The trial has to use the ugly records and not a cleaned sample.

Sixth we reread the research as a brake. Gartner says 63% lack the practices or are unsure they have them. It expects 60% of unsupported projects to be abandoned through 2026. It also says at least 50% of generative projects were abandoned after the first test run. That was by the end of last year. Those figures are reasons to refuse a test that flatters the record, so we do not resize them.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is calling an export the one place the facts live. The scheduler can pull a schedule file any morning. By the time the crew lead is in the yard, the file is a souvenir. The right place is whatever will still be correct when the customer calls at the end of the day. If that turns out to be the crew lead's head, say so out loud.

Another mistake is cleaning the data for the demo. Tidy jobs are not the business. A first test run that only sees them will pass. Then it will fail when poor data quality shows up. Use a record you are a little ashamed of.

A third mistake is treating a lot of history as readiness. Old invoices in a folder are documents. If no system can read them, a person retypes them. You are in the middle row no matter how many years the folder covers. Volume is not a source.

We also watch owners skip the person who knows which fields are wrong. The owner knows the approval column goes stale. If he is not in the conversation, the tool will treat that column as fact. The research can talk about data quality. In the room it is a person with a grudge against one specific field. Find that person.

The last mistake is citing a sample size that these pages do not give you. We do not cite the sample size of the February 2025 page. The article and its structured data do not agree on it. Please do not fill that gap with a number you heard somewhere else.

## What we'd do

We would not buy the drafting tool for the owner yet. First the yard note and the approval must live in one place a message can read. We hold that opinion firmly. A smoother voice on a split record is how you send a confident update that the crew lead would not sign. The customer will not blame the data model, and will blame the crew.

If we were the owner, we would pick the update job only. We would make one shared note the place where the crew lead's sentence and the yes on extra work land the same day. We would leave the spreadsheet alone until it matches that note. Then we would try a tool on a messy yard. If we still could not name the place the facts live, we would stay on the low-data guide. We would keep the money. One current record is the requirement, and a warehouse can wait.

## AI Strategy for Small Business: Start With the Job

An AI plan for a small business is a short list you can say out loud. It names the job that changes, the facts it needs, and the person who checks the work. It is not a list of tools, and it is not a big speech about the future. If your page cannot name those three things, you have a pile of apps and a hope that the pile will turn into a plan.

The [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) scores the same groups of facts we want on that page. The [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework) is the order of work once the job has a name. The [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is the score sheet under both of them. We start with the job. The tools can wait in the other room until the page exists.

We have watched owners skip the page because it felt too small to matter. In a company this size, a good plan is one job that still works in a busy week. A thick binder that covers every department you do not have is just for show.

## Use is ahead of the plan

Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work.[^microsoft] Of those users, 46% started less than six months before the survey. Also, 60% of leaders worry that their company has no clear plan for how to use AI. About 78% of AI users bring their own tools to work. At small and midsize businesses, that goes up to 80%.

Leaders also worry about finding talent, and 55% said so. Yet only 25% of companies were planning to offer training on generative AI. We read that as a truck cab and a front office that have not met yet. People already use the tools. But the plan, the training, and the hiring worries are all behind them.

NIST's risk framework groups the work into four parts called Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.[^nist] A plan that cannot point to those four parts has not really started. Govern means who is allowed to decide. Map means where the work and the facts live. Measure means how you will know when the answer is wrong. Manage means what you do in the week it is wrong. If your page is only a list of product names, it skips all four.

<!--image:2-->

Salesforce asked 3,350 leaders at firms with 200 workers or fewer.[^salesforce] The survey ran in August and September 2024. About 75% said they were at least trying out AI, and that rose to 83% among growing small and midsize businesses. Among growing firms, 78% planned to spend more on AI. Only 55% of the firms that were shrinking did. Of the leaders who already used AI, 91% said it helps their revenue. Those are leaders talking about their own companies, so we will not repeat the claim as if your revenue had already agreed.

<!--cta:inline-->

These numbers come from different groups of people. Microsoft asked knowledge workers and leaders, while Salesforce asked small business leaders. Neither one can take the place of a job you can name on a single page. A worker who brings a tool from home and a leader who says revenue went up can both be telling the truth. They are just answering different questions. Your page still has to pick one job.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Picture a heating and cooling company that runs a handful of trucks. This is only an example, and nobody measured it for a report. The owner prices jobs from the driver's seat. He has started pasting notes about a broken unit into a chatbot on his own phone. He likes the draft it gives him, but he has not told the dispatcher.

The dispatcher builds the day's board from calls, texts, and a whiteboard that is more right than the software they pay for. Two techs trust the board. They do not trust a long message the owner forwards at night.

So there is no plan yet, just people quietly using their own tools. That is the same habit we saw in the Microsoft numbers, where most AI users bring their own tools and even more do at small and midsize businesses. The owner is not a bad guy. He found something that helps him write a quote when he is tired. The trouble starts when a customer reads the draft back to the dispatcher the next morning. It names a part the shop does not stock and a price the owner would have changed at a desk.

The office manager finds out in the worst way, which is from the customer. She has no page that says which jobs the tool may touch. She has no rule that a quote only leaves after she or the dispatcher has seen it. Nobody trained her, because there was nothing to train on except that the boss has an app. The low training numbers from Microsoft will sound familiar to her. She lives in the gap between using the tool and having a plan.

Here is the page we would write with them, and it still has no tool name on it. The job is to draft estimates for swap-out jobs. It is not for complaints or anything that sounds like a safety problem. The facts come from the price book on the office computer and the notes the tech already puts on the ticket. They do not come from the owner's memory of a house that looked similar. The dispatcher checks the draft, because she already knows which crews can do the work this week. When she is out, the office manager takes her place, and both names are written down. If a draft names a part they do not stock, it does not go out. That is a real plan, and it is short enough to tape inside a cabinet door.

We also left some things off the page on purpose. We did not write that the company will look for ways to use AI everywhere. We did not put a chatbot on the website. The techs need the board to stay right. The owner's late night drafts can stay only if they become drafts the dispatcher expects, built from facts the office already trusts. Until then, the honest rule is to stop forwarding the chat to customers.

## How we'd run it

We build the page before we add a login, because the order matters more than the paperwork.

First, we ask the owner what he already does in private. The chatbot in the truck is a fact, so we write it down and we do not scold him for it. We call it bring-your-own use, which is common. We keep it apart from a company plan, which is not. A habit that stays hidden is risky. But once we name it, we can change it.

Second, we pick one job and draw a fence around it. Swap-out estimates are inside the fence. Complaints, safety calls, and anything the price book cannot back up are outside it. The fence is the plan. A job with no fence turns into every job by Friday, because the tool will answer any question you type. Being able to answer is not the same as having permission.

Third, we name the facts and the checker in the same meeting. For this company the price book and the ticket notes are in, and the owner's memory is out. The dispatcher checks, and the office manager covers. We put time on the dispatcher's calendar so that checking is a real slot and not just a good idea. This is where the Map and Measure parts of the NIST framework live, even if we never say those words in the room. Govern is the owner agreeing that the fence is real. Manage is what they do when a draft breaks the fence. They hold it back and say the reason out loud once, so the techs hear the rule.

Fourth, we train only the people named on that page. That means the dispatcher and the office manager, working on this one job with real tickets from last week. We do not hold an all-hands talk about the future of the trades. Only 25% of companies in the Microsoft survey planned any training on generative AI. We would rather be in that group for one role than outside it with a pep talk. The techs get a simpler lesson. Quotes to customers come from the office and not from a forwarded chat.

Fifth, we leave the revenue claim alone. Salesforce heard leaders say that AI helps their revenue, including a large share of those who already used it. We will not print that on this company's page as if it were their result. Their result, if they earn one, will be a dispatcher who can clear draft estimates without a surprise part. If they want a score before they start, the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) and the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) are the sheets to use. If they want the order of work after the page exists, that is the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework).

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is writing the plan as a shopping list, which is what the sellers hope for. A list of products is not a job, a place for facts, or a checker. It is a stack of bills. In the Microsoft survey, 60% of leaders already worried that their company lacked a plan for AI. A shopping list will not calm that worry. It will only add more logins.

The second mistake is pretending that bring-your-own use is not happening. About 78% of AI users bring their own tools, and that is 80% at small and midsize businesses. Your owner in the truck is normal. If the plan ignores him, he will keep forwarding drafts, and the plan will describe a company that does not exist. You can fold his habit into the plan, or you can ban it in one sentence he agrees with. But please do one of the two.

The third mistake is training the staff in a vague way, which keeps the training imaginary. The people who need it are the dispatcher and the office manager. A general session lets everyone nod and changes no ticket. The Microsoft numbers show that training plans were rare, and copying that gap is easy. A short lesson on one job is the fix.

The fourth mistake is borrowing another group's revenue number. Of the Salesforce leaders who already used AI, 91% said it helps their revenue. They run firms with 200 workers or fewer, and the survey ran through August and September 2024. They are free to say that about themselves, but you should not treat it as your forecast. The 75% who were at least trying AI, and the 83% among growing small and midsize firms, still describe leaders and not your whiteboard.

The last mistake is skipping Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage because the names sound like a big institution. The names are just drawers. They ask who decides, where the facts are, how you notice a bad answer, and what you do next. A heating company can fill those drawers on one page. If it will not, the plan has not started, no matter how new the owner's app feels.

## What we'd do

We would tape one page inside the cabinet, and we would not start any tool until the page has names on it. That is the view we bring into the room. Use is already ahead of the plan. In the Microsoft survey, 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work, and 46% of those users had started less than six months before they were asked. The plan is the thing that is hard to find. Chasing more use, when you already have use in the truck, is how you stay among the 60% of leaders who worry they have no clear plan. We would make the plan a fence around one job.

We would not tell this owner that AI helps revenue just because 91% of the leaders who already used it said so to Salesforce. We think leaders answer surveys about their own story. We do not think that story carries over to a dispatcher who has not seen the draft. About 78% of growing firms planned to spend more, against 55% of the firms that were shrinking. Spending without a checker is how a shrinking firm gets a new bill. We would spend on the price book, the dispatcher's time, and a rule the techs can repeat.

We would also be plain about talent. In the Microsoft survey, 55% of leaders worried about it, and we share a smaller version of that worry. You probably do not need a new kind of worker. You need the dispatcher to be allowed to say no to the owner's draft. That is a people choice dressed up as a software choice. If you cannot give her that right, do not buy anything. Go back to the [readiness framework](/blog/ai-readiness-framework) until she has it. Then the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework) can run, and the [assessment](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) will have something real to score. A plan that the dispatcher can spoil is a real plan. A plan that only the owner understands is a hobby with a title.

## Answer Engine Optimization: What Google Still Requires

Answer engine optimization is the work of getting cited when an AI writes an answer. Google still treats that work as ordinary search work, so the new name does not give your site a new set of rules.

Google's guide says the work is still the same old search work.[^google] The page has to be in Google's list of pages, and it has to be able to show a snippet, which is the short piece of text Google puts under a result. Google says it does not use llms.txt, which is a plain file some people add to a site to tell AI tools what to read. It also says there is no special way you must cut up your text. And no extra hidden labels in the page code are needed for these features. We turn that into a short list of things you do not get. You do not get a magic file that makes you the answer. You do not get to hide the real page behind a block of text a person cannot read. What you do is plain. You publish a page Google can list, a page a snippet can lift from, and a page a customer can finish.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) is the matching check for whether the site can be cited at all. The [ChatGPT note](/blog/how-to-get-your-business-to-show-up-in-chatgpt) covers crawler files, which are a different switch from this one. The [GEO comparison](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) puts the research and the click study side by side, if you want to see both.

## What the research measured

A 2024 paper on generative engine optimization reports visibility gains of up to 40%.[^geo] Methods that add citations, quotes, and facts with numbers were linked to gains of more than 40%. On Perplexity, which is an AI search tool, the gain reached 37%. A score for how much of the answer came from the page rose 41%, and a score for how useful the answer felt rose 28%. The test used ten thousand questions. Those results come from pages written to be easier for an AI answer to lift from. They do not promise that your faucet page will move by a set amount because you added a quote.

When we sit with an owner, we take one thing from the paper. It is the kind of sentence that got the lift. A citation points at a source. A quote is a real person saying something you can check. A number with a clear group behind it is a fact the answer can carry. A page that says "we are the best hardware store in town" has none of those. A better page says how a cartridge is measured, quotes the maker's note on fit, and tells the reader which handles in the aisle match it. The gain is tied to that kind of writing. It is not tied to the phrase "answer engine" in the footer.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Pew, in July 2025, found that people clicked a link 8% of the time when an AI summary showed up.[^pew] When no summary showed up, they clicked 15% of the time. A citation that nobody clicks is still a citation. But you should write the page so the click is worth taking.

Owners feel that drop at the till, even if they never see the study. If the summary already told the person the cartridge size, they may not need you for that fact. They still need you for the part in stock and the person who will show them the wrench. They also need an honest line about what you will not do on a Sunday. Put that on the page. The summary can borrow the size, but the visit is for the counter.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Walk into a hardware store on your street. This is an example we talk through, and it is not a result. One person works the counter and knows which aisle has what. People already ask a question like this, out loud and in search: can someone cut a key and tell me which cartridge fits my dripping faucet?

The old page says the store sells hardware, paint, and keys. It has a phone number and a cheerful line about friendly service. Google barely lists it, and a snippet would have nothing sharp to lift. An AI asked about that faucet will cite a page that states the size, the common mix-up, and what to bring to the counter. The owner's page can be that page. But it will not get there by adding a new acronym to the title.

What the counter lead knows is the raw material. He already tells the person holding a bag of old parts that the stem length matters more than the brand on the handle. He also says a photo of the old cartridge saves a second trip. That line belongs at the top, in words a summary can quote and a person can use. Under it, the owner writes what the store really does. They cut keys while you wait on the days the counter lead is in. They match cartridges if you bring the old one or a clear photo. They do not fix pipes inside the wall. That last line is useful because it keeps the answer honest. It also keeps a click from turning into a sad visit.

Each person has a clear job. The owner owns the claims and will not let the page say they repair what they only sell. The counter lead checks the draft against what he says at the counter, because a polished sentence that does not match him will annoy the next customer. Whoever updates the site, even if that is a nephew, has one job. The page must stay listed, the first sentences must answer the question, and the source of any number must be easy to see. If a number is about their own stock, the page says it is theirs. If it comes from a maker's sheet, the page names the sheet. That is the same move as the paper's citations and quotes, done at the size of one shop.

An AI answer might then say the stem length matters and send the person to the owner. Pew's finding is why the page cannot stop at the fact the summary will take. The summary can explain the stem, but the page has to make the trip better. Bring the old cartridge. The counter lead is the one who matches it. The store does not open the wall. Those lines are the reason to click, and they also keep the citation from turning into a complaint.

## How we'd run it

We would not start with a tool that "does answer engine work." We would start with the page a customer already lands on, and we would ask whether a stranger could act on it.

First, we check that the page is in Google's list and can show a snippet. If it is blocked, thin, or tucked behind a form, we stop there. Google's guide is blunt that these features still need an ordinary page. No special file can take the place of one.

Second, we write the question in the customer's own words at the top, and we answer it in the next sentences. That might be key cutting, a cartridge match, or what to bring. A heading that repeats the question helps a person scan the page, and it gives an answer something clean to lift. This is plain structure and not a special ritual. Google says it has no special rule for how you cut up the text.

Third, we add the kind of material the 2024 paper linked to the gains. That means a real citation, a real quote, and a real number. For the owner, that might be the maker's fit note, a sentence that really came from the counter lead, and a plain list of the sizes they stock. We do not invent a study. We also do not borrow a number we could not defend if a customer read it back to us.
