Fourth, we add the reason to click, knowing a summary may already have stated the fact. That means the hours in words, what you will not do, who does the matching, and what to carry in. Pew's July 2025 read is the background here. People clicked 8% of the time when a summary showed up, against 15% when it did not. So we write for the person who still has a reason to come.

Fifth, we skip the extras Google says it does not need. We do not wait on llms.txt. We do not add hidden labels in the page code that we cannot explain. We do not chop the page into scraps that only a machine could love. The person in the aisle is the reader who can hurt you.

Sixth, we read the page out loud at the counter. The counter lead fixes anything he would not say, and the owner deletes any boast. Then we leave the page up long enough to see whether the questions at the register start to match the questions on the page. At this size, that is the feedback that counts. A visibility score from a vendor is nice to have, but the counter is not optional.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is treating the new name as a new channel with its own file. Google says this is still ordinary search work, and it says it does not use llms.txt. A shop that spends the week on a special file and leaves the faucet page vague has done the opposite of what the guide says.

The second mistake is a page that nobody can lift from. It has no clear answer in the first lines and no heading a person can scan. Its only real fact is a phone number. Being able to show a snippet is a rule and not a matter of taste. If a snippet would be empty, an AI answer will be empty too.

The third mistake is fake precision. The paper's gains were up to 40%, and above 40% where citations, quotes, and numbers were added. Those gains describe methods on a test of ten thousand questions. If you paste those percentages into the owner's title, you tell a lie about her store. Use the method, but do not wear the result.

The fourth mistake is writing only for the summary. You polish the fact and forget the click. When a summary was there, Pew saw a click 8% of the time, against 15% without one. A perfect citation that sends nobody to the counter makes for a thinner business, even if a dashboard calls it visibility.

The fifth mistake is a page that says one thing while the counter does another. The page promises same-day key cutting. But the counter lead is off that day, and the backup will not touch the machine. The AI cites you and the customer shows up. Then you lose the one thing that mattered, which is being believed next time.

The sixth mistake is extra hidden labels as a superstition. The guide says no extra labels are needed for these features. Adding code you do not understand will not fix a page that never answered the question.

## What we'd do

We would rewrite the one page people already need, in the counter lead's own words, with the refusal included. We would ignore the pitch that this is a separate craft with a separate invoice. Our view is that the paper is useful and the label is not. The gains in a 2024 study are a reason to put citations, quotes, and numbers on the page when you truly have them. They are not a reason to talk differently from the way you talk at the counter.

Google still wants a listed page that a snippet can use. Pew says the click gets rarer when a summary shows up. So the page has to be worth the trip after the answer has already spoken. We would rather the owner be cited for a true line about stem length and then earn the visit. That beats chasing a file Google has said it does not read. If you do one thing after this, open the page that should win the question and see whether a stranger could follow it. That is the work. The acronym can wait in the hallway.

## Business Process Automation With AI: Write the Job

Business process automation with AI starts with a written job. We mean the steps a person already follows, in order. We also mark the spot where they use their own judgment. An AI model can't follow a job that lives in someone's head. It will make up the missing steps, and the made-up steps will sound very sure of themselves. Anthropic's December 2024 essay says to start with the simplest thing that works. It also says to keep a fixed list of steps until the next step truly depends on what the last one found.[^anthropic] We treat that as everyday advice. The tool comes after the page, and if the page is blank, the tool is just guessing.

If the steps are not written down, stop spending money. The [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-mid) is the matching fix for that blank page. The [automation note](/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business) helps you pick which job to start with once you can see more than one. The [agents note](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) covers a later question. It asks what to do when a fixed list is not enough, because the next step depends on what the last step found. An AI agent is a tool that picks its own next step. Most of the rooms we sit in are not ready for that yet. People are still telling the work from memory, and the story changes each time we ask.

## The process is the product

The map is the thing you are making. Software is only a way to run that map the same way on a busy Tuesday as on a quiet Monday. Microsoft's 2024 index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI, and 46% of those users started less than six months earlier.[^microsoft] Using AI is already normal, but having a shared plan is not. Leaders worry about this, since 60% of them say their company lacks a plan and vision. Another 55% of leaders were worried about finding talent. Only 25% of companies were planning to teach people how to use AI. People are already in the tools, and almost nobody is showing them a shared way to work.

Your staff are probably using AI already, with or without a plan. Among AI users, 78% bring their own tools to work, and that number is 80% at small and midsize businesses. At a small firm that often means a personal login the owner likes and a different tab the office manager likes. The work lands in the shared inbox, but the method stays in a browser history. When that person is out, the method is out too. That is not a process, because it is only a habit with a password. If you ban the login without writing down the path, the habit just moves somewhere else.

The place where the hours go should decide which job you write first. People spent 60% of their time in the work apps on email, chat, and meetings, and 40% on making new things. Owners often want to automate the part that feels like making something, and they leave the inbox alone. But the inbox is the job, and so is the chat thread. So is the meeting that ends without a note. Making new things is the smaller share of the day. So we sort the daily mess before we polish a rare piece of writing.

<!--image:2-->

Gartner's January 2026 article says at least 50% of generative AI projects were dropped after the first test run by the end of the year before. It names poor data, weak risk checks, rising costs, and unclear value as the causes.[^gartner-fail] We don't read that as a reason to fear the tools. We read it as a picture of demos that never had a job attached. Poor data shows up when nobody decided which record is the real one. Weak risk checks show up when nobody owns the stop button. Rising costs show up when the test keeps growing because the goal was never one written path. Unclear value shows up when you can't point at the step that got easier to finish. Then the project is dropped, and the report blames the model. The missing page never makes it into the report.

<!--cta:inline-->

Write down the steps a person already follows. Mark the step that waits for a judgment, and automate the steps that don't. If every step needs a judgment, you don't have a process yet, you have a craft. A craft can still get help at the edges, such as drafts, reminders, and a place for the file to land. But it should not be sold a machine that pretends to replace the judgment. We would rather say that on the first call. Then nobody pays for a pilot that looks just like the pile Gartner described.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a trades desk as the example we walk through. This is not a measured result and it is not a trophy story. It is the shape of the afternoon we keep seeing when we ask someone to tell us about yesterday. The owner prices the work and the office manager answers the phone. A lead tech visits the site and comes back with a note that is half measurements and half memory. The bookkeeper sends the invoice only after someone says the job is done.

Yesterday's quote starts as a voicemail. The office manager jots down the name, the street, the room, and a mention of a leak. The lead tech visits and takes photos on a personal phone. Then he texts a few of them to the owner with a line saying the job isn't bad. The owner opens an old quote, changes a few lines, and sets the price from a similar job they remember. The bookkeeper never sees any of it until the customer says yes. Sometimes the yes arrives as a text to the owner, who means to forward it and forgets.

When we sit there and write the path, it becomes ordinary in the best way. The office manager logs the address and the room before the visit is booked. The lead tech files the measurements and the photos before leaving the driveway. The owner prices the job from that note, and the price is the step that waits for a person. The office manager sends the quote only after the price is on it. The bookkeeper opens the invoice only after the yes is written down. We would not hand the price to a model. The rest is copying, ordering, and waiting for a mark. A simple system can carry the note, remind the tech about a missing measurement, and hold the quote. A person still sends it. What the bookkeeper wants is usually small. It is a written yes, a matching price, and the same spelling of the name on the invoice. That is a handoff.

A clinic has the same shape with different words. The front desk takes the call, and the practitioner decides whether the visit is something they can help with. Billing waits for both. Once those steps are written, the front desk can draft the confirmation while a person still sends it. If nobody writes them, someone buys a tool that claims to handle intake. Meanwhile the practitioner keeps a side pad that becomes the real process. A shop counter looks simpler, which is why owners skip the page. The Saturday clerk and the owner tell two different stories when we ask each of them how a reorder really happens. We write both versions down before anyone opens a settings screen.

## How we'd run it

First, we ask the person who did the job yesterday to walk through it without making it better. We want the version that happened, including the text message and the sticky note. We write their words where they can see them. We don't clean them up yet, because cleaning is how wishes sneak in.

Second, we ask another person who touches the same job to walk through it too. The office manager and the owner almost never tell the same story. Where they disagree, we don't blend the two into a polite middle. We ask which version the customer actually got, and that version wins because the customer is the only one who paid.

Third, we write the steps as short sentences that a new hire could follow on a tired morning. Each sentence names a person and the thing they make. The lead tech files the measurements before leaving the driveway, for example. If a sentence has no result, it is not a step but a mood, and moods can't be automated.

Fourth, we mark the step that waits for a judgment. On the trades desk that step is the price. At the clinic it might be whether the visit is something they can take on. At the shop it might be whether a regular customer gets a refund after the posted window. If we can't find the mark, we are not ready to automate anything. We don't yet know what has to stay with a person.

Fifth, we automate only the steps that don't wait. We move the note, remind the person, hold the draft, and file the photo. We use the simplest thing that makes each move. A fixed list of steps is enough when the next step doesn't depend on a surprise in the last one. The quote either has a price or it doesn't, so that is a gate and not a thinking problem. We stay with the gate even when a vendor calls it an agent.

Sixth, we run the written path on live jobs while the old path is still allowed. Then we watch where people step around it. The workaround is the missing step, so we add it to the page. We don't scold the person who stepped around, since they are showing us the job we failed to write. We keep a named person on the send button. The system can prepare the draft. But the words that reach the customer go out because someone with a name looked at them. Without that, you just have a mailbox that talks.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake we see is buying a tool because a neighbor bought one. The neighbor's job is not yours, and their judgment may sit in a different place. We once sat with an owner who bought a stack of seats. Nothing was connected to a real quote, and the owner called the quiet that followed a failed pilot. The pilot never had a page, and the bill for the seats still arrived.

The next mistake is writing down the process you wish you had. The wished-for version has no voicemail and no promise to remember, but the real version is made of those things. If you automate the wish, the staff will keep the real path in a group text while the new system sits empty. Then people blame the staff for not using it. Really, the page described a company that doesn't exist. We write the messy path first, and then we remove one mess at a time once it is visible.

Another mistake is automating the judgment because it hurts, which has the best sales pitch of all. Pricing hurts, and so does deciding whether a visit is in scope. Telling a customer no hurts as well. But pain is not a sign that a model should own the step. We move the chores around it and leave the painful step with a named person. If the owner wants that step gone, we ask a question. What will you do when the model is wrong in front of a customer? If the answer is a shrug, we don't build it.

It also wastes time to treat personal tools as a moral failure. The share of people who bring their own tools is just a fact. At small and midsize businesses that share is higher. If you ban the personal login without a shared path, people will find another login. So give them the path, and then show it on a real job. Teaching, which few companies were even planning, is how the path survives the first busy stretch.

Calling a first test run a strategy is how budgets disappear. A test run checks a written step, and with no step you only have a demo. When the value stays unclear, the project joins the dropped pile. Leaving out the person who lives in the path is the same mistake in a quieter voice. If the office manager was not in the room, the map won't match the phone. If they stumble while reading a sentence aloud, the sentence is wrong.

## What we'd do

We would say no to the model until the steps fit on one page. A person who does the job should nod at each line. We hold that view even when the owner is eager and a vendor is already waiting in the hallway. Being eager is not a process, and a demo in the hallway is not a process either. A pile of licenses is not a process either. The page is the process, and everything else is a way to run it.

We would pick the job that already happens every day in email, chat, or the meeting note. That is where the hours already go. We would mark the judgment and keep a named person on it. A fixed list of steps can carry the rest. We would not start with an agent or a custom build. If the next step truly depends on what the last step found, we can talk about something smarter. First, someone has to show us that branch on a real job from last week.

We would also say the quiet part about teaching. People are using these tools, and few companies were planning to show them a shared way. A path that nobody is shown on a real quote is like a folder nobody opens. If you want a test before you spend anything, ask yesterday's doer to write the steps from memory. Then ask the person who receives the result what they wish they had received. If those two pages don't match, you have found the work, and you can name a product after that, not before.

## Generative Engine Optimization vs SEO

In Google's own guide, generative engine optimization and SEO are the same craft. The page still has to be worth reading by a person. The idea that you must pick a side is a sales pitch, and it is not how the guide is written.

Google says answer-engine optimization and generative-engine optimization are still SEO.[^google] The page has to be in Google's list of pages, and it has to be allowed to show as a snippet. Google does not use llms.txt, and it does not ask you to chop the page up in any special way. We keep those lines together because owners are being told to pay for a second program beside the first one. The guide does not describe a second program. It only describes the page you already owed your reader, which is now being quoted inside an answer.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) is how you check whether that page can be found and quoted. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) lists the methods in one place, if you want them. The [llms.txt note](/blog/what-is-llms-txt) covers the file Google says it ignores. That is good to know before someone sells it to you as the gap between the two names.

## What changes, and what does not

The 2024 paper says that pages written for a generated answer gained up to 40% in how often they showed up.[^geo] Adding quotes, sources, and facts with numbers went with gains of over 40%. On Perplexity the gains went up to 37%. The study also saw a 41% rise in word count, adjusted for position. It saw a 28% rise in how the reader felt about the answer. All of this came from a set of 10,000 questions. So what changes, in that study, is how easy it is to spot a source inside the answer when the writing carries proof. What does not change is the need for a real page that a robot can read and a person can use.

Keep the two layers apart when a pitch blurs them. SEO, the way Google uses the word, gets the page into its list and ready to be quoted as a snippet. The generative layer is what happens when an answer borrows from that page. You can fail the first layer and never reach the second one. You can also get quoted and still fail the business, if the quote told the reader enough and the visit never came. Both failures belong to the same page, so they are not two departments.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Pew found, in July 2025, that people clicked a link 8% of the time when a search showed an AI summary. When it showed none, they clicked 15% of the time.[^pew] SEO still gets the page into the list, and the page still has to be worth the click.

That is the plain split we want owners to remember. Getting into the list is the price of a seat. The click is what pays for the chair time, the staff, and the front desk. A page written only to be summed up will do the first job and skip the second. A page that is only a thin list of keywords will do neither one well. A summary has nothing solid to lift, and a person has nothing solid to trust.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a small dental clinic as an example, and not as a case with a score. The front desk lead already answers the same questions that people type into the search box. The dentist will not let the website make up promises about care. The questions the owner cares about are the ones new patients ask before they call. They want to know what happens at a first visit. They ask whether it is okay to bring up a cracked tooth. They also ask whether the clinic will see someone who is nervous.

The page they have today is an SEO page in the old, thin way. It has a city name, the words "family dentistry," a list of services, and a map. It might be in Google's list, but a snippet from it would be mush. Say someone asks an answer engine about a cracked tooth and a nervous patient. It will skip that page for one that says what the first hour is like. That other page tells you what to bring and what the clinic will not promise. The owner does not need a second site for these readers. She only needs this one page to do both jobs.

What does not change is the floor. The page has to be in Google's list and ready to show as a snippet. The front desk lead should be able to read the first lines and say, "Yes, that is what I tell people." The dentist should be able to read the clinical lines without wincing. If those two cannot sign off on the page, no engine should be quoting it. Google's no to special chopping and to llms.txt fits here too. Breaking the page into bits does not help, and neither does adding a side file. Nothing takes the place of the owner standing behind each sentence.

What changes is the shape of the sentences. The paper is why we say so, though we will not turn it into a promise. In that 2024 work, quotes, sources, and facts with numbers went with gains of over 40%, on a set of 10,000 questions. For this clinic, the honest version is small. Quote the after-care steps you already hand out on paper. Name the rules you really follow when you talk about a cracked tooth, and skip the blog that only sounds like a doctor. If you give a number, it should be one you can explain. A patient may read it in an answer and walk in holding it. Word count and the reader score moved in the study, by 41% and 28%. We do not make those a goal for the owner. We turn them into a simple rule, which is to write enough real detail that a reader can feel the visit before they book.

The click problem sits on top of that. Pew is why we will not let the page stop at what a cracked tooth is. A summary can explain the tooth, but the page has to explain this clinic. First visits start with a talk and not a surprise procedure. Nervous patients can say so when they book, and the front desk lead will set aside a longer time in the chair. The clinic does not do every kind of care, and it will say which kinds it sends elsewhere. A summary that only wanted a definition has no use for those lines, and they are the reason a person still taps through. In the July 2025 Pew look, people clicked 8% of the time when a summary showed, against 15% when none did. So write the lines the summary cannot cover.

Now the jobs again, because this is where projects get sloppy. The owner approves what the clinic claims. The front desk lead checks the practical lines against the phone script, including the list of places the clinic sends people. The dentist owns anything that could sound like a diagnosis or a promise of no pain. A freelancer can tidy the headings, but a freelancer cannot decide where the clinic sends people. Say the generative work and the SEO work are billed as two projects. You will get two drafts that disagree, and the patient will find that out at the front desk.

## How we'd run it

We would run one page, one time, for both names.

First, pick the one question the front desk lead answers every week, and write about only that. It might be a first visit, or a cracked tooth, or how the clinic treats a nervous patient, with one page for each question. A page that tries to be the whole clinic will be quoted for nothing in particular.

Second, make the SEO basics easy to see. The page should be in Google's list, open to anyone without a login, and ready to show as a snippet. It should also start with sentences that answer the question. If a snippet of those lines would embarrass the dentist, they are the wrong lines. Fix them before you worry about any generative layer.

Third, add proof the way the 2024 paper describes it, but only proof you really have. That means a source you would show a patient. It means a quote that is truly yours, or the steps you already print. And it means a number you can defend. The study saw gains of up to 40% when pages were written for a generated answer. It saw gains over 40% tied to quotes, sources, and numbers. On Perplexity the gains went up to 37%. Use the method on your own material, and do not paste the study's percentages onto the clinic.

Fourth, write for the click. Say what the summary will not know. Tell people how booking works with the front desk lead and what to bring. Say what you refuse to do, and which fear you will take seriously. This is the reply to Pew, because being the source is not the same as being visited.

Fifth, say no to the split invoice. Do not hire one firm for SEO and another for generative work on the same page unless they edit one document. Two plans make two tones, and the answer will quote whichever is cleaner, which may be the one the dentist never saw.

Sixth, read it the way the desk will hear it. The front desk lead reads the practical half out loud, and the dentist reads the clinical half. Then the owner asks, "If this is the only paragraph a summary keeps, is it still true?" If the answer is no, cut until it is. Then publish the one page. The names GEO and SEO can both point to it, but they do not each get a website.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is thinking the two names are rival crafts. Google says they are still SEO, so a clinic that stops its normal work to "move to GEO" has misread the guide. A page that Google has not listed will never be the quoted source.

The second mistake is the side file. Google does not use llms.txt for this. If you buy a file, or a service that starts with the file, the first-visit page stays vague. You have spent the week on the part the guide shrugs off.

The third mistake is adding special structure for its own sake. Google asks for no special chopping of the page. Headings that match real questions help people, and they give an answer a clean edge to lift. Headings that are only bait, with nothing under them, help no one. We would rather see four plain sections a patient can scan than a pile of bits.

The fourth mistake is using the study as a forecast for your town. The paper reports gains of up to 40%, over 40% with quotes, sources, and numbers, and up to 37% on Perplexity. It also reports a 41% rise in word count, a 28% rise in reader feeling, and a set of 10,000 questions. That is what the paper measured. It is not the owner's sales line, and putting it on the homepage would be the wrong kind of number.

The fifth mistake is ignoring the click. Pew's 8% with a summary, against 15% without, is the business problem hiding inside the win. You can win a mention that takes the place of the visit. Put the detail that a summary cannot hold on the page, like the person, the things you refuse, and how booking really feels.

The sixth mistake is having two owners for one page. One person edits for keywords and another edits for answers, and neither sits with the front desk lead, so the patient meets the gap. We want one page, one checker at the desk, and one dentist who can veto a line.

## What we'd do

We would keep a single page and a single editor, and we would drop the idea that GEO replaces SEO. Our view is that the guide is right and the fight over names is not. Write the page so a person can use it. That is what makes it ready for Google's list, ready for a snippet, and worth quoting. The 2024 paper says that proof on the page goes with more reach inside generated answers. Pew says the click gets harder once a summary shows up. Both facts point the same way. Be clear enough to be quoted, and rich enough in detail that the quote cannot say it all.

We would spend the owner's money on the front desk lead's questions and the dentist's veto, and not on a second strategy deck. If a firm cannot show the same page doing both jobs, they are selling a fight that Google did not ask for. The page still has to exist for the list of links and for the quoted answer. So make it true first, then make it useful. Leave it where a robot and a nervous patient can both find it.

## How Can AI Help a Small Business? What Surveys Count

AI helps a small business when it takes over a named job that a person already does. It does not help by moving you closer to a headline. Two surveys from 2025 count AI in small firms, and they count different kinds of work. The U.S. Chamber asked who uses generative AI. Statistics Canada asked who used AI to make goods or to deliver services. A firm can say yes to the first and no to the second, and both answers can be honest. This note keeps those two claims apart, and then it names the jobs that owners hand over. The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) asks the matching question for one business, and we write these notes on [our site](/).

We sit with owners who have already been told they are late. The number they heard was usually the bigger one. So the first thing we do is find out what that number really measures. Help, for a shop or a clinic or a trades desk, looks like a draft that someone checks. It looks like a sort that someone trusts, or a reminder that someone still sends. It is not a rank on a national chart.

## Generative use is not production use

The Chamber's small business report says 58% of small businesses called themselves users of generative AI.[^chamber] That is up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. That question is about generative AI. It does not ask whether AI makes the goods or the service. The owner said so, and no one watched the work to check. It also does not mean the tool is part of the product. An owner who drafts a customer email and then rewrites half of it can answer yes. We would answer yes with them. That yes is real, but it is a different fact from a system that makes the thing the customer bought.

Statistics Canada ran its Canadian Survey on Business Conditions for the second quarter of 2025. It found that 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services.[^statcan] That is up from 6.1% in the second quarter of 2024. The release is dated 16 June 2025, and the survey ran from 1 April to 5 May 2025. The agency got 21,357 responses, and 9,103 of them came from businesses that used AI. Read those counts as a picture of who was asked, and not as a target. A big response still describes the questions that were asked. It does not turn the generative question into the production question.

<!--image:2-->

Among the businesses that used AI, 35.7% used text analytics and 23.1% used marketing automation. Then 40.1% had made new workflows, and 38.9% had trained their staff. Those shares sit inside the group that already uses AI. They are not shares of every firm in the country, and they are not shares of the Chamber's question. Text analytics means reading and sorting words. Marketing automation means sending messages and counting what comes back. A new workflow is a path that was not written down before. Training means a person was shown that path. Put that way, the list is practical, and it is also modest. None of the four says the business now runs itself.

<!--cta:inline-->

## Jobs an owner can hand over

The Chamber number describes a tool that someone opens. The StatCan number describes AI inside the making of the product or the service. A small business can do the first for a long time without ever doing the second. We think that is a sane order. Open the tool on a job you can check. Ask the production question later, when the goods or the service truly depend on the system. Most owners we sit with are nowhere near that later question, and they do not need to pretend they are.

The jobs in the StatCan list are the practical ones. They are reading and sorting text and sending and measuring marketing. They are also writing a workflow that did not exist and training the people who will run it. None of them is a promise that the tool will run the business. Reading text looks like an inbox, a pile of referrals or a supplier sheet. Sending marketing looks like a note to people who already bought from you. It is not a brand campaign with a film crew. A new workflow looks like a page the front desk can follow. The owner can be in a room with a patient at the time. Training looks like sitting with that person once on a real message. It does not look like a slide deck made for a big company.

The [readiness note](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) asks a different question. It asks whether this firm has the data, the process, the people and the decision in place. It does not ask about the average firm. Average firms are what surveys are for, but your firm is a counter, a desk and a schedule. If the readiness questions fail, the survey numbers will not save the project. If they pass, you still do not need the bigger number as a goal. What you need is the job.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a clinic as the walkthrough. The owner saw the Chamber number and felt late, because friends in a group chat were already using it. The front desk still types appointment reminders by hand. The practitioner still scribbles the note after each visit, and billing still waits for someone to say the visit happened. Nothing in that room makes care through a model. The care is the practitioner. The model may come in at all. If it does, it comes in as a draft of a reminder. Or it comes in as a cleaner version of a note that the practitioner will still sign.

Walk the reminder first, because it happens every day and a wrong one is easy to spot. The front desk has the visit in the book. A draft can say the time, the place and what to bring. The front desk reads it, because some patients need a phone call and some need a short message. The draft does not know the difference. The practitioner is not in that choice unless the reminder holds a clinical instruction, and then the practitioner reads it. Billing does not need to see it at all. That is three roles and one job, and we named the handoff.

A shop down the street is even plainer, which is why the headline feels insulting there. The owner sorts supplier mail and customer questions in the same inbox. Sorting is text work, so a system can group the supplier sheets away from the sizing questions. The owner still decides which question gets an answer before lunch. The goods on the shelf were not made by a model. If the shop says it uses AI because the inbox got grouped, that is the Chamber kind of yes. If it said it uses AI to make the goods, that would be the StatCan question. The honest answer would be no.

A trades desk sits between the two. The lead tech's site note is text, and turning it into a description the customer can read is a draft. The owner still sets the price, and the service is still the repair. You are near the production question only when the job truly depends on the system. A friend forwarding a chart does not count. Until then, hand over the draft and keep the price.

## How we'd run it

First, write down which survey sentence you heard. If it was about generative use, say so in a full sentence. If it was about making the goods or the service, say that instead. Owners often mix the two into "most businesses are already doing this," which is not what either source said. The groups are different, and the Canadian production share is the quieter fact.

Second, name one job on your floor that matches the practical list. It might be reading and sorting, or a message you send more than once. It might be a path that is not written down, or a person who has not been shown the path. Pick the one that already hurts this week. Do not pick the one that would look good in a post.

Third, write the roles the way we wrote them for the clinic reminder. Say who drafts, who must read, and who is left out. If everyone is involved, you do not have a handoff, because you have a meeting. Training means showing the person who will really run it.

Fourth, keep the output in a waiting place until the named person acts. A reminder waits, and so does a sorted inbox and a rewritten note. The send, the order and the published page stay with a person. They stay there until you can say what happens when they are wrong. For a clinic, wrong means a patient came on the wrong day. For a shop, wrong means a regular got a cold note. For a trades desk, wrong means a price the owner never set. If you cannot say what wrong looks like, you are not ready to let the draft travel.

Fifth, wait until that job has been dull for a while, and then ask the production question on purpose. Does the good or the service depend on this system? Or does a person still make the thing while the system handles the words around it? If a person still makes the thing, you are in the generative pattern. That is a fine place to stay. The smaller production share is not a scolding. It is a count of a harder change.

Sixth, check readiness for this firm and not for the average firm. You need data you trust and a process someone can say out loud. You need a person who will own the check, and a choice about what not to automate. The readiness note is that talk, and the pressure guide asks where the business really hurts. Neither one is a national percentage.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we fix most often is blending the two surveys into one mood. The Chamber series shows a rise in owners who say they use generative AI. The Canadian series shows a much smaller share using AI to make goods or deliver services. It also shows what AI-using firms changed afterward. Those two are neighbors and not twins. If you quote one, you tell a different story than the speaker told. We have heard pitches that borrow the bigger number and then promise the smaller number's result. That is how a draft tool gets sold as a new way to deliver the service.

The next mistake is treating a yes from an owner as a finished operation. An owner who tried a chatbot on a Sunday can say they use it. The front desk may never have seen the login. The survey cannot see that gap, because it asked the business and not each role. When we sit down, we ask the person who does the job and not the person who read the article. If those two answers differ, believe the doer.

Reading the tool shares as a quota is how small firms buy things they will not run. Text analytics and marketing automation are common among the Canadian firms that already use AI. But common is not the same as required. A clinic with no marketing program does not need a marketing project just so a share looks familiar. A shop that never posts a page does not need a content stack. The workflow share and the training share interest us more than the tool shares. They describe the work after the tool arrived. A firm that adopted a tool, never changed the path and never showed anyone is the firm we worry about. We worry even if its yes was confident.

Skipping the group is how 9,103 starts to sound like a club you failed to join. That count is responses from businesses that used AI. It sits inside a larger set of responses, in a survey with a set window of time. It is not a count of businesses that have figured out your counter. Use it to remember that the claim has a base, and do not use it as a mirror.

The last mistake is letting the headline pick the job. The owner wants whatever the article seemed to praise, but the floor wants the reminder or the inbox. We follow the floor. The article already gave us clean questions, and it does not get to staff the front desk.

## What we'd do

We would tell the owner the bigger number and the smaller number in the same sitting. We would attach the question to each. We would also refuse to pick a tool until they can say which question they truly care about. Most of the time they care about a job and not about production. That is our opinion, and we think it is the kinder one. If you chase the production share before the reminder is reliable, you buy a system. The practitioner will then work around it.

We would hand over reading and sorting first, because the inbox is already there. We would keep a person on anything a customer could feel. We would write the workflow only for the job we just named. Then we would train the person who runs it before anyone else. A slide for the whole staff can wait, but the front desk cannot.

We would not use either survey as a score for the firm in front of us. Surveys measure everyone, and the readiness questions measure you. Write the job the way the customer feels it and name the person who checks it. Then ignore every percentage until that sentence exists. The percentages will still be true in the morning. Your counter is the thing that can slip.

## How to Show Up in ChatGPT and AI Overviews

Getting a business into ChatGPT search starts with the right crawler. That is not the same one OpenAI uses for training, so a mix-up here can undo all the other work. If we block the wrong one, or block all of them, the writing never gets a chance to matter.

OpenAI says it runs separate crawlers.[^openai] OAI-SearchBot fetches pages for search results. If you turn it off, your pages stay out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot is the crawler for training. ChatGPT-User fetches a page when a person asks for a look-up, and robots.txt may not apply to that one. These are three different jobs, and we repeat that until the owner can say it back to us. Most robots files treat every bot as the same thing. So a rule written in a hurry mixes them up. The mix-up is quiet, because the page just never shows up and someone blames the writing.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) reads the site the way a practical check should. It starts with whether a crawler can see the pages at all. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) and the [generative-engine note](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) cover the names people use for Google's summaries. This note stays on the switches, and on the page those switches are meant to show.

## What Google says to do

Google's guide for its generative features says the work is still SEO.[^google] It says answer-engine work and generative-engine work are both SEO from where Google sits. It says Google does not use llms.txt. It also says there is no special rule for how to chunk a page. The page has to be indexed, and it has to be able to show up as a snippet. No extra schema is needed for these features either. If you came here only for ChatGPT, please do not skip this part, because many owners want both. The Google half of the job is still an ordinary page. A special file will not stand in for it on either side.

<!--image:2-->

Say a page is blocked, thin, or not allowed to show a snippet. It will not turn into an overview because someone added a new file. So we let the search crawler in and keep the page open to indexing. Then we write the answer where a person can read it too.

We see this go wrong in a pattern. First, an agency blocks every bot "for safety," including the search crawler. The owner hears that the site is now protected. Then someone adds a new file because a thread said that file is how you show up. The page underneath is still a list of cities and a phone number. Nothing in that story gives a homeowner an answer they can use. The crawler has to be allowed to fetch. The page has to be open to indexing, and the sentences have to be worth repeating. The file is not the sentence.

<!--cta:inline-->

Pew found, in July 2025, that visits with an AI summary led to a click 8% of the time. When no summary showed, it was 15%.[^pew] That means showing up is not the same as being clicked. So we write the page so that the citation is worth the click.

The Pew study is about Google's summaries, but the habit is the same, so we bring it in here. A generated answer can cover the easy part of a question and leave you unvisited. If you win the mention and lose the call, you have only done half of the job. The page has to carry the part a summary cannot finish. That means who sends the truck, what you will not touch, and how a person books.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Picture an electrical contractor with us. This is a made-up scene, and it is not a measured result. An office manager runs the office, the inbox, and the site password, and two techs do the work. Homeowners ask whether someone can look at a panel that keeps tripping. They also want to know if that person is licensed and insured. And they want someone honest enough to say when the problem is on the utility side.

Their site today is a header, three service words, and a contact form that sometimes fails on a phone. The office manager once pasted a robots file from a forum. A post there said AI companies were copying the web. He did not know he had turned away the crawler that fetches pages for search. Then the owner paid for a rewrite. It added a file at the root and left the service page as thin as before. They were told it would help them show up, but it did not. The search crawler was still shut out, and the page still had nothing a citation could honestly repeat.

So we would split the switches the way OpenAI splits them. OAI-SearchBot has to be allowed if ChatGPT search is going to fetch the panel page. Blocking it keeps the page out of those answers. That is a fair choice if the owner does not want to be there, and a mistake if she does. GPTBot is the training crawler, and that is a separate decision. The owner can say no to training and still want search. She cannot say that with one "disallow all" line she does not understand. ChatGPT-User is the third case, because it fetches when a person asks and robots.txt may not apply. The office manager should know that rule exists. Then he will not tell the owner that a robots file controls every look-up a user can start.

The page itself has to work for a person standing in a dark kitchen. The opening lines answer the panel question. Then they say what you do on a trip and what you will not do. That includes anything on the utility side of the meter. They also say how to reach the office manager. And they say what to tell her so the right tech brings the right tester. The techs should know the description when they read it. They are the ones who will hear "but your website said" in a hallway. The owner signs off on the claims about license and insurance. The office manager signs off on the crawler rules, in writing. The three bots are named in words he can point at.

A generated answer might then mention the firm for a tripping panel in their towns. That mention is not a booking, and Pew is the reminder, even though it measured a different summary. When a summary is on the screen, a click is less common. So the paragraph that the answer cannot replace is the one about the utility line. It also covers calling the office manager with a photo of the panel label. The citation makes them curious, and the clear refusal gets them to the phone. A thin page only gets them a sentence that could have been about any electrician in the county.

## How we'd run it

We would fix the robots file and the service page in the same week. We would not call a new root file the project.

First, write the three crawlers in the office manager's notebook in plain words. OAI-SearchBot fetches pages for search, and leaving it blocked keeps you out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot is for training. ChatGPT-User fetches when a person asks for a look-up, and a robots file may not control it. If the office manager cannot tell them apart yet, nobody edits the file.

Second, decide the training question on purpose. Some owners want no training crawl, and that is allowed, but it is not the same lever as search. Then make the search choice out loud. Maybe the owner wants to be found in ChatGPT search. Then OAI-SearchBot has to be allowed to fetch the pages she hopes will be cited. We write the decision next to the file. That way the next freelancer does not "clean it up."

Third, look at the Google basics on the same pages. Each page should be indexed, able to show a snippet, not blocked, and not thin. The only useful sentence should not hide behind a form. Google's guide says the generative features are still SEO. It does not use llms.txt, and there is no special rule for chunking. No extra schema is needed. A page that fails these basics will not become an overview because a file appeared.

Fourth, rewrite the service page in the voice of the kitchen, and not in the voice of a keyword list. It should cover the panel question and the utility line. It should also say what to photograph and how booking with the office manager works. A person should be able to read it without feeling sold to. An answer should be able to lift a sentence without making up the rest.

Fifth, add a reason to click. We assume the summary took the easy meaning of a tripping breaker. So we leave the shop-specific part on the page. That means who comes, what you turn down, and what a homeowner should have ready. Pew saw a click 8% of the time when a summary showed, against 15% when none did. Showing up is the citation, and the click needs its own writing.

Sixth, test it the boring way. Ask someone who does not work there to find the page from the question. They should use a phone, and then tell you what they would do next. If they cannot say, the citation will not save you, so fix the page. After that we leave the crawler rules alone unless the owner changes her mind. A steady file matters more than a monthly tweak from whoever read a thread last.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is one switch for every bot. A copied robots file that blocks everything will block OAI-SearchBot along with GPTBot. You have then opted out of search answers and called it privacy. If privacy was the goal, that is fine. If the goal was to show up, you closed the door and then paid someone to decorate it.

The second mistake is the magic file. Google says it does not use llms.txt. A page that is blocked, thin, or not able to show a snippet will not become an overview because a new file was added. We have heard the file sold as the ChatGPT trick as well. The real trick is the right crawler plus a page worth citing. The file is just a list at best.

The third mistake is a page that only a model could love. It has fragments, repeated town names, and no sentence a tech would say out loud in a hallway. There is no special chunking rule, and headings are for people who scan. Would a tech be embarrassed to read the page to a customer? Then it is the wrong page, however well a crawler can fetch it.

The fourth mistake is mixing up a mention with a call. The July 2025 Pew finding is the warning. Visits with a summary led to a click 8% of the time, against 15% without one. We write the line the summary cannot finish. That is the edge of the work, the photo to send, and the person who answers.

The fifth mistake is making claims nobody will back. One example is "same hour" when the truck is across the county. Another is "we repair utility equipment" when you do not. ChatGPT-User may fetch the page because a person asked, and robots.txt may not apply. So a careless sentence can travel even when you thought you had a gate. We write only what the owner will say in the driveway.

The sixth mistake is handing the file to someone who cannot name the bots. The office manager should own it, or a person he trusts who will explain each change in plain words. An anonymous plugin update that "optimizes robots" is how the search crawler gets shut out again on a Friday.

## What we'd do

We would allow the search crawler and make a separate, clear choice about training. Then we would spend the real effort on the panel page that a homeowner can use. We would not start with a root file. We would not let a single disallow line stand in for a decision. Our view is that most "show up in ChatGPT" projects are a robots accident. Add a thin page with a strategy name on top, and that is the whole project.

Google still wants an indexed page that a snippet can lift. It still turns down the special file and the special schema. OpenAI still uses different crawlers for search, for training, and for a fetch a person starts. Pew still says clicks get thinner when a summary is already on the screen. Those three facts are the whole job. Let the search crawler in if you want to be cited. Write the answer where the office manager, a tech, and the homeowner would all know it. Then make the next step so clear that a citation has somewhere to go.

## How to Use AI in Your Business: Twelve Jobs

Using AI in a business starts with a list of jobs, not a list of tools. Pick a job you already do and write down the steps. Then keep a person on the result. The tool is the last thing you choose, and for many jobs it is a small one.

Statistics Canada asked businesses that already use AI which tools they use and what they changed.[^statcan] In its 2025 report, 35.7% of them used text analytics, which is software that reads and sorts written text. Another 23.1% used marketing automation. Also, 40.1% had built new ways of working, and 38.9% had trained their staff. In the same report, 12.2% of all businesses used AI to make goods or give a service, up from 6.1% a year before. These numbers show what firms said they did. They are not a shopping list, so there is no reason to open twelve tools on Monday.

The [help note](/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) explains the gap between making goods with AI and using AI to write and sort. The [automation note](/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business) shows how to pick the first job. The [agents note](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) covers the time when the steps start to branch, and a fixed checklist no longer fits. We'd start with one job from the list below. Then we'd leave the rest alone until that job has a person on it and a week of real use behind it.

## Twelve jobs you can write down

In each job below, AI does the first try and a person makes the call.

- AI drafts the customer reply, and a person sends it.
- AI sums up the meeting, and a person accepts the tasks.
- AI turns notes into a quote, and a person sets the price.
- AI sorts the inbox, and a person decides what gets an answer.
- AI flags the late bill, and a person decides how to chase it.
- AI describes the product, and a person approves the page.
- AI groups the help requests, and a person picks the answer.
- AI spots the stock problem, and a person places the order.
- AI rewrites the policy in plain words, and a person posts it.
- AI compares two supplier notes, and a person chooses.
- AI drafts the weekly report, and a person accepts the numbers.
- AI prepares the staff answer, and a person trains the staff.

Every line has the same shape. The tool gets the work ready, and a person decides. If you take the person out, you no longer have a job. You have a mailbox that hopes for the best. The reply can be drafted from the thread the customer wrote, but someone who knows that customer still sends it. The meeting summary can list the tasks, but someone who was in the room still accepts them. The tool was not there to hear the aside that mattered. The quote can be built from notes, but the price stays with the owner. We keep coming back to this shape because owners try to skip the second half, and the second half is the business.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

The numbers above are about businesses that already use AI, except the 12.2% figure. That one covers all businesses in the Canadian survey. So please don't read the text analytics share as a share of every firm. When we say 35.7%, we mean that share of the businesses already using AI, not the shop on the corner. Marketing automation at 23.1% is the same kind of share. The 40.1% and 38.9% for new ways of working and training are also among firms that already use AI. They tell you what those firms changed. They don't say that a firm that has never tried this is behind, and they don't say which of the twelve jobs to run first. The 12.2% figure stands apart, and we don't want it mixed in with the others. Using a tool to draft a reply is a different claim from using AI to make the goods or give the service.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a shop we keep using as our walkthrough. It is not a case study or a scoreboard. It is just a counter, a back room, and three people. The owner buys and sets prices, a clerk covers the floor and the inbox, and a bookkeeper chases what was not paid.

Yesterday, in this story, looked like any other day. A customer emailed about a size, and a supplier sent a new price sheet. Two bills sat past the date the bookkeeper cares about. A talk with the landlord left a page of scribbles and no tasks. The product page for a new item was still blank. None of that needs a new company, but someone does need to say which of those is the job for now.

Say they pick the customer reply, because it comes up every day. A wrong tone with a regular costs more than any chart can show. The clerk drops the thread into a draft. The draft pulls in the size the customer asked about and the line the owner uses for delays. The clerk reads it and changes one sentence, because this customer dislikes cheery notes. Then the clerk sends it. The tool did not know about the cheery notes, but the clerk did, and that is the whole design.

You can sort the inbox in the same pass if you like. A person still decides what gets answered today and what can wait. The late bill goes on a list the bookkeeper already trusts, and the bookkeeper decides how to chase it. A stiff note to a good account takes good sense. A reminder to a stranger who has been quiet for sixty days is closer to a rule. Even then, we like a person to take a quick look.

The quote job shows up the day the shop does custom work. Notes from a talk become a description, and the owner sets the price. We've watched owners let the draft set the price because it sounded sure of itself. But sounding sure is not the same as knowing the cost. The supplier comparison is the same trap in a different coat. There are two notes with two minimums and two lead times, all written in different ways. A draft can line them up. The owner chooses, because choosing is the job and lining up is only the chore.

A clinic can run the same list without acting like a shop. The practitioner accepts the tasks from the meeting summary, and a person trains the staff on the answer the tool prepared. A person also posts the plain-word policy. That step matters because a policy that sounds friendly but says the wrong thing about care is worse than a stiff one that is right. A trades desk lives in the quote and the stock problem. The lead tech's note becomes a description, and the owner sets the price. Then a person checks the problem and places the order. We are not saying every firm should run all twelve. We are saying that each of the twelve is a job with an edge, and the edge is a person.

## How we'd run it

First, write the twelve down where the owner can see them, in the firm's own words. "Flag the late bill" might mean "the Tuesday list the bookkeeper already prints." So use that name for it. A job you can't say in their words is not a job you can hand over.

Second, pick one with a simple test. It should happen often, the result should be easy to check, and a mistake should show up before a customer gets hurt. The customer reply and the late bill flag usually pass that test. The weekly report often fails it, because a wrong number becomes the record if nobody is named to accept it. So if you can't name the person who accepts the numbers, don't start there.

Third, write the steps of that one job the way it happened yesterday, not the way a brochure tells it. Say who gets the message and who is allowed to send. Say what done looks like and where the draft waits. If the draft doesn't wait, you skipped the design.

Fourth, run it on live work with the old way still allowed. The clerk can still type a reply from scratch. You are watching to see if the draft gets good enough that they stop wanting to. If they keep typing from scratch, then either the draft is wrong or the job was the wrong one. Fix that before you add a second job.

Fifth, name the person who checks, in a sentence another worker could read. It might say, "The clerk sends customer replies, and the owner sends anything with a price or an apology." That sentence will save you more pain than a new tool. Group the help requests the same way, so the tool groups them and a person picks the answer. Describe the product the same way, so the tool drafts and a person approves the page.

Sixth, only then look at a second job. The pattern in the survey that we trust is not the tool share. It is the pair of follow-up moves, which are new ways of working and staff who were truly trained. The 40.1% and 38.9% are shares among firms already using AI, and even there they are not everyone. A second job with no new steps and no trained person is how the first job dies. So leave the rest alone until the first job feels dull.

## Common mistakes

Starting from a list of tools is the mistake the title is about. Someone asks which chatbot to buy before they can say which reply they want drafted. The tools will pile up, but the jobs won't get any clearer. We've sat at tables where three logins were already paid for. Nobody could point to a sent reply that had passed through any of them. The money was small, but the mess was not.

Treating the survey as a ranking of your firm is the next one. A text analytics share among AI users is not a grade. The 12.2% for making goods and giving services is a different question, and it is smaller for a reason. Most of the help open to a small firm is still a draft, a sort, or a summary. That is fine, but calling it "AI in the product" when it isn't will send you chasing a build you don't need. The help note walks through that gap. Use it before you scare yourself with the small figure or flatter yourself with the large one.

Skipping the person on the result is the mistake that reaches the customer. A drafted reply that goes out alone will sooner or later be warm to the wrong person. Or it will be sure about a price the owner never set. A weekly report that nobody accepts will be quoted in a meeting as if it were the books. A policy that is rewritten and posted unread can change what staff think the rule is. The second half of every line in the list is there because we have seen the first half travel alone.

Running all twelve at once is impatience dressed up as ambition. A shop that tries replies, bills, stock, the product page, and the staff answer in the same month will do all of them badly. Then it will decide the tools don't work. But the tools were never given a job, only a pile. So pick one and let it get boring, because boring is what success looks like here.

Forgetting training is how the survey figure and the real room come apart. A new way of working that lives only in the owner's head is the old business with an extra tab. Show the clerk on a real thread and the bookkeeper on a real late bill. If the only person who can run it is the person who set it up, you don't have a job. You have a hobby.

## What we'd do

We'd pick the customer reply or the late bill and turn down every other job for a while. That is our view, because twelve examples are still only a list, and a list doesn't run the counter. One checked job does. We'd write the steps in the clerk's words and put their name on the send. Then we'd sit with them once on real mail before we called it done.

We wouldn't buy a second tool to cheer the first week. We wouldn't hand the quote price to a draft because the sentences looked finished. We wouldn't post a rewritten policy just because it sounded friendly. And we wouldn't read 35.7% as a target for our shop, since it is a share of a different group, in a Canadian survey, among firms that already use AI. It works as a map of what those firms touch, but not as a quota.

If you do nothing else after reading this, circle one line from the twelve and write the name of the person who finishes it. If you can't circle one, you don't have a use yet. You have curiosity, which is a fine place to start and a poor thing to automate. The question about goods and services can wait until a job you already do has a person on the result and a path someone else could follow.

## Is My Business Ready for AI? Signs to Read First

A business is ready for AI when one named job can move to a tool without anyone inventing the process along the way. Ready is not a mood, and it is not a purchase. It describes the data, the process, the people, and the decision around that one job. If any one of those four is still a shrug, then the job is not ready yet.

The [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) scores this as four bands. Early is 0–39, Forming is 40–59, Ready is 60–79, and Running is 80–100.[^check] Each sentence on the check describes a state of the business. The check does not diagnose anything, and we like that limit. A diagnosis invites shame, but a state invites the next piece of work. Early is allowed to be the true state. Plenty of good businesses are Early on the job they just tried to automate, and they are fine at the rest of their work.

The [Early band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/band/early) and the [Ready band](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/band/ready) spell out those states in full sentences. The [assessment note](/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) compares the public tools side by side. Read the band pages when you want the exact wording. Read this note when you want to know which signs to trust before a vendor tells you what the signs are.

## What a large-firm index is counting

Cisco's 2025 AI Readiness Index surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at organizations with more than 500 employees, across 30 markets and 26 industries.[^cisco] The firms it called pacesetters were near 13% of that sample, and they were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production. That sample is not a census of small businesses. So a small firm can be Ready on our check and still look nothing like a pacesetter.

We say that last part slowly, because owners often miss it. Ready on our check means the named job can carry a tool. A pacesetter in Cisco's index is a large organization in a sample of senior leaders, and the 13% describes those organizations. It is not a report card for a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk. Suppose a salesperson says you should buy now to catch up with the pacesetters. Then they have glued a large-firm statistic to a small-firm fear. The 4 times gap in moving pilots into production is real inside that sample. It does not mean your service writer is late.

Use the index as a picture of a different size of firm. The useful part is that moving a pilot into production follows a written process. The useless move is to decide you are behind a business that staffs a whole crew for its pilot. You have a bay, a desk, and a person who knows the customers. Readiness is whether that person can hand the job to a tool without the job falling apart.

<!--image:2-->

The OECD SME AI adoption tool is part of 2026 Group of Seven work. It is a short self-check for smaller firms.[^oecd] It takes about five minutes, keeps the answers in the browser, and does not publish an adoption rate. We'd use it as a second set of questions and not as a national share. A second set helps because our own questions can go stale in our own mouths. Someone else's short check, with no stored data and no pretend rate, is a good way to see whether you dodged a theme. It will not tell you whether small firms in your country are ready. If someone finishes it and announces a countrywide rate, they have added a sentence the tool refused to say.

<!--cta:inline-->

We look for four signs that a job can move to a tool. The one place the facts live has a name, the steps are written down, a person owns the output, and someone can stop the experiment. We also look for four signs that it cannot move. The knowledge sits in one head, the exceptions are unwritten, nobody may send the output to a customer, and success has no definition.

The signs are easy to see when the person who does the job is in the room. "Named" means you can point at one record, and the other records lose the argument. "Written" means a new person could follow the exceptions and not only the sunny path. "Owns the output" means a human is accountable for what a customer receives. "Can stop" means someone may halt a bad send without asking the vendor.

The bad signs are the same facts turned around. Knowledge in one head feels like loyalty to a great employee, but it also means the job stops when that person is out. Unwritten exceptions feel like flexibility, but they are where a tool will start to improvise. Nobody being allowed to send feels like caution, until you notice that someone is already sending from a personal account. And success with no definition is how a pilot turns into a subscription.

<!--image:3-->

A small firm can show the good signs on one job and the bad signs on another. That is normal, and it is why "is my business ready?" is the wrong question. The honest question is which job. The check's bands describe the state you are in, based on how you answered, and they are not a tattoo on the business. Early and Forming are 0–39 and 40–59, and they are descriptions. Ready and Running are 60–79 and 80–100, and they are descriptions too. None of them means you have bought a product, and none of them means you have failed as an owner.

## A worked example

Say we are in an independent auto shop on a slow afternoon. One person writes the service tickets, and another is the lead tech. This is an example we walk through, so we are not reporting their revenue, how often cars come back, or any other number. We did not measure those, and we will not fake them.

The owner asked after a vendor showed a tool that drafts customer updates from the ticket. We split the question and asked which job she meant. The job on offer is the status text. The lead tech finds what is wrong, the customer hears it and says yes or no, and then the lead tech goes ahead or does not.

Walk the good signs. Is there one place the facts live, and does it have a name? The ticket writer says it is the shop system. The lead tech says she writes the real finding on the paper that stays on the dash. The system ticket holds only what the ticket writer had time to type, and he is often still with the last customer. The owner says she trusts whatever the ticket writer texts her. That makes three candidates, so the source is not named, and that is the first bad sign already. The true finding sits on the lead tech's paper and in her head, which is the "one head" sign, even though the ticket writer has a system. A system that nobody believes is not the one place the facts live.

Are the steps written down? The sunny path is written, and it goes car in, inspect, call, approve, repair, car out. The exceptions are not written. What if the customer does not answer and the bay is needed? What if the lead tech finds a second problem after the yes? What if the ticket writer is off and the other writer does not know the lead tech's shorthand? Those are unwritten exceptions, and that is the second bad sign.

Does a person own the output? The vendor's tool would send a text, and the ticket writer assumes he would glance at it. The lead tech says she would not see it until the customer called angry. The owner says she wants to approve "the important ones," which means there is no rule. So nobody owns the output in a way that survives a busy morning, and that is the third gap.

Can someone stop the experiment? The owner says she could cancel the subscription. That stops the bill, but it does not stop the day's work. A real stop sounds like this: this text does not go out today because it is wrong. The person who sees that may halt it without a meeting. The shop does not have that person yet, and that is the fourth gap.

So the shop is not ready for this job, and that is not an insult. The owner runs a respected bay. The signs say the status text would invent a process that the ticket writer, the lead tech, and the owner do not share today. If we put the same shop on the check, we would not be surprised to see Early or Forming. We would be surprised, and a little suspicious, if the answers came back Ready while the dash paper still beats the ticket.

What would ready look like, without pretending we watched it happen? The ticket writer and the lead tech agree that the ticket is the record. The dash paper becomes a scratch pad that gets typed in before anyone is texted. The no-answer case and the second-problem case are written where the other writer can find them. The ticket writer owns the text. The lead tech can reject a finding that is not what she saw, and the owner can halt a wrong text the same day. Success means the customer hears the finding the lead tech actually made. That is Ready in the ordinary sense, and it does not look like a pacesetter. It looks like a shop that stopped inventing the process inside the tool.

## How we'd run it

First, we refuse the wide question. "Is my business ready?" becomes "is this job ready?" The owner does not get to mean the whole shop. She gets the status text, because that is what the vendor is selling. A yes about a different job is a way of changing the subject.

Second, we read the large-firm index for what it counted, and then we say out loud that the shop is not in that sample. The fear of being behind the pacesetters does not get a vote.

Third, we walk the four good signs and the four bad signs as pairs. Is the source named, or does it sit in one head? Are the steps written, or are the exceptions loose? Does a person own the output, or is nobody allowed to send? Can someone stop the trial, or does success have no definition? The ticket writer, the lead tech, and the owner each answer, and we write down the conflicts instead of smoothing them over. The lead tech's paper against the ticket writer's ticket is the conflict that matters.

Fourth, we open the band pages if a label will help. Early and Ready are states with sentences, and they are not prizes. If the signs are bad, we expect Early or Forming. We treat a Ready result as a reason to reread the answers, not as a reason to celebrate. The check does not diagnose, and neither do we.

Fifth, we use the OECD self-check as a second pass. It takes about five minutes, the answers stay in the browser, and there is no adoption rate to misuse. If it shows a theme we skipped, we add that theme. If someone tries to turn it into "small firms are behind," we stop them, because the tool did not say that.

Sixth, we talk about the vendor only after the signs are honest. If the signs are bad, the meeting ends without a quote. If the signs are good for this one job, we still name who stops the trial before anyone creates a login. Ready includes the brake.

## Common mistakes

The mistake we see most is hearing "ready" as a personality. The owner is decisive, the lead tech is skilled, and the ticket writer is careful. None of that answers the signs. A careful writer with two records is not ready for a tool that needs one, because character is not a band.

Another mistake is using Cisco's 13% as a small-business failure rate. It is the share of pacesetters in a sample of large organizations. Quoting it to scare a shop owner mixes up two different kinds of firm. The sample is not a census of bays and storefronts, and we will not nod along when a pitch says otherwise.

A third mistake is counting the cancel button as the ability to stop. The owner can always call the vendor later. What we want is someone on the floor who can block a bad customer message today. Later is how a wrong text sits in a customer's phone all afternoon.

We also see owners collect the good signs as adjectives and skip the bad ones. They can name a system, so they ignore that the lead tech does not believe it. Naming a system you do not trust is the one-head problem in a nicer outfit. So look at the bad list on purpose, because it is ruder and it is clearer.

The last mistake is treating the OECD tool's missing rate as bad news. It does not publish an adoption rate, and that is restraint. Do not fill the silence with a guess and then feel behind the guess.

## What we'd do

We would answer the owner with the signs and not with a pep talk. Most shops that ask "are we ready?" are really asking for permission to buy. The honest answer is often that one job is Forming and the rest of the question is too big. We would rather shrink the question than inflate the readiness.

If we were the owner, we would make the ticket the only record the lead tech is willing to have texted. We would write the no-answer case where the other writer can see it. We would also give the lead tech a plain way to kill a message that does not match her finding. Then we would take the check and read the band as a state. If it says Ready, we would still start with one job and a person who can stop it. If it says Early, we would believe the dash paper over the demo.

## Off-the-Shelf AI or Custom Software

Off-the-shelf AI is the right buy when a product already does the job. Custom software is the right build when the job is special to how your business works and no product covers it. We start there because owners usually start at the other end. They hear that serious firms build, or they hear that nobody should build. Both speeches skip the one question that matters. Does a product already do this job, with a person you can name checking the output? If yes, buy it. If the job depends on your records, your exceptions, and your checker, a product will not make those up for you. That is the custom case, and it is rarer than the sales talk suggests.

The [studio](/) takes the work that products do not cover. The [consultant note](/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business) covers what to ask before you pick either path. The [agency comparison](/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) covers who to hire once you know you are building. It also helps if you know you should not be. We would rather lose a build than make a custom frame for a job that a sealed box already does. The box is not an insult. The box is how a small firm stays small instead of becoming a software company by accident.

## What the surveys count

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023.[^chamber] That is a claim about use. It is not a claim that those firms built their own software. Use can mean a tab someone opened, or a draft written inside a product they already pay for. The rise over those years says owners are trying the tools. It does not say they hired anyone to build something new. When a pitch borrows the 58% and then offers you a custom build, it has quietly changed the subject. The subject was use, but the bill is for a build, and those are two different purchases.

<!--image:2-->

Salesforce asked 3,350 leaders at firms with 200 employees or fewer.[^salesforce] In that survey, 75% were at least trying out AI, and 83% of growing small and midsize businesses said the same.
