Among firms already using AI, 91% said it boosts revenue. The survey does not say whether those tools were bought or built. Read that last sentence twice before you let a revenue line pick your plan. "At least trying out" is a very wide door. A revenue boost among people already using AI does not name a vendor. It does not name a pile of code you will have to feed, either. We have heard that revenue line used as a reason to build, but the line has no idea what was bought.

<!--cta:inline-->

If a bought product covers the job, buy it. If the job depends on your records, your exceptions, and your checker, the product will not make those up, and that is the custom case. Records means the files you really keep, not the files a demo pretended you had. Exceptions means the customer you treat differently and the job you turn down. The checker means a named person who can say the output is wrong. If you miss any one of the three, you do not have a custom case. You have a wish that someone will design your business while they design the software.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take a shop whose reorder list already lives in the register. This is a walkthrough, not a result. The owner gets a flag when a staple item runs low, and the Saturday clerk trusts that flag enough to pull a box. The bookkeeper does not need a second opinion unless the flag is about a special order. A cousin in another trade told the owner to "build something with AI" after seeing a demo. Building here would mean a second list that drifts away from the register. It would also mean a login the clerk will not open on a busy Saturday. And the new list still could not tell a staple from a special order any better than the flag can. So keep the product you have, and spend your time on the one exception the flag gets wrong. Write down who decides that exception, and you are done. It might be a setting, or it might be a sentence on the wall, but it is not a custom build.

A trades desk is where we stop saying buy so quickly. A quote starts as a voicemail. Then it becomes a site note, picks up photos from the lead tech's phone, and waits for the owner to set a price. The office manager sends it only after the price is there. No product they already pay for holds that whole stack. The accounting tool holds the invoice after the customer says yes, and the inbox holds the mess before that. A bought AI assistant can draft a friendly note and still lose the measurement. Custom, in this room, means a path that keeps the measurement, the photo, and the price gap together until the owner fills the gap. The price stays a gap on purpose, because we will not build a system that makes up a price. If a vendor says their shelf product already does the whole path, make them run yesterday's quote in front of you. If they can, buy it. If they redraw your job until it fits their screens, you are back in the custom case. Or you are in the case where you change your job to fit a product. Changing the job is allowed. Pretending you did not change it is how the build gets blamed later.

A clinic usually looks like the shop until someone describes intake. Plain reminders are a product, and many booking tools already send them. Do not order a reminder engine just so the waiting room can say you built something. The custom candidate is the odd part of intake. That might be the practitioner's rules about which visits are in scope, or the note that billing needs. It might be the patient who must be called instead of messaged. If those rules live only in the practitioner's head, a product will not make them up. A custom build would only lock in a bad guess. Write the rules down first, and then see whether a product has a place to put them. Only the leftover is a build. We have watched clinics jump to the leftover and then find that the booking tool had a field for it all along. The field is not glamorous, and glamour is a poor reason to hire a developer.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job as one sentence with a person on the output. The clerk acts on the reorder flag. The owner sets the price after the note is complete. The front desk sends the reminder after reading it. If the sentence has no person in it, you do not yet know what you are buying or building. You are really just shopping for a good feeling.

Second, list the products you already pay for and ask, in writing, whether any of them do that sentence. Ask the person who uses the product, not only the person who gets the bill. The bookkeeper knows whether late invoices are already flagged. The clerk knows whether the reorder flag tells the truth. The front desk knows whether reminders already go out. A consultant helps here when the owner is too close to the demo to see the product they already have.

Third, try the shelf product on yesterday's real job before you talk to a builder. Do not use a sample record. Use the awkward one from yesterday, like the special order, the quote with the missing measurement, or the patient who has to be called. If the product handles the awkward one with a person checking it, stop there, because you have your answer. Custom work that starts before this trial is how you end up paying to find a checkbox.

Fourth, if the product fails, write down the exact miss. It might be "it cannot hold the site photo with the measurement." It might be "it has no place for the practitioner's scope rule." That sentence becomes your spec. A builder who will not repeat the sentence back to you is about to build a different job, one their tools happen to like. The agency comparison only matters once that sentence exists. Before it, an agency is just a team making a guess.

Fifth, name the checker for the thing you buy and for the thing you build. A shelf tool with nobody checking it is still a risk. A custom tool with nobody checking it is a costlier risk, because you now own the repairs. The revenue line in the Salesforce survey is not a stand-in for that name. A boost among people already using AI does not tell you who presses send.

Sixth, decide what you will not maintain. Custom software is a long relationship with your own exceptions. If nobody on the desk can describe an exception a year from now, do not put it in code. Leave it as a human step. The cheapest system is the one that refuses to swallow a judgment call. We like that kind of cheap because it keeps the owner in the business they meant to run.

## Common mistakes

One mistake is hearing "most small businesses use AI" and turning it into "most small businesses built their own." The Chamber figure feeds that mistake all the time. The 58% counts use, and use went up over the years in that report. Use can be a login, a draft, or a feature inside something you already rent. We have had to say this in rooms where a relative had already told the owner that renting was naive. Renting a product that does the job is the grown-up move. Building a second copy of the register is the naive one, even though it wears a very serious face.

Another mistake is letting a revenue line pick your plan. Of firms already using AI, 91% said it boosts revenue. That is a report about users, not a promise about your custom build. It does not split bought tools from built ones. A shop can see a lift from a better reminder inside a tool it already has. A trades desk can see nothing from a custom portal that the office manager dislikes, and the survey cannot see that dislike. You can. The numbers 75% and 83% mean a lot of people are trying things, but trying is not a blueprint.

A third mistake is building a solved job because custom feels like owning something. That is how small firms end up with a second business they never wanted. Code you have no time to feed is a cost that looks like an asset in the proposal. The proposal shows a tidy system. The Tuesday after launch shows a clerk who still uses the register, and a new system that pings you when a field is empty. You will end up fixing both, and the cousin who suggested the build will not help.

A fourth mistake is skipping yesterday's awkward job, which makes the trial lie. Teams test the easy path, and the easy path fits every product. Your business lives in the exceptions, like the refund you allow, the visit you refuse, and the price you will not put in an email. If the trial never touches those, you learned nothing. You watched a demo with your logo placed near it. Ask for the awkward one. If a seller will not run it, believe them, because they just told you the product does not cover the job.

A fifth mistake is freezing unwritten rules into custom software, and it feels a lot like progress. The practitioner's scope rules are not on any page, so the builder asks about them for an hour and codes up that hour. Next month a case shows up that the hour never covered. Now the software is confidently wrong, and fixing it is a whole project. A product with a blank field would have been more honest. Write the rule until a new hire could follow it, and then decide whether it needs software at all.

## What we'd do

We would buy first, and we would be stubborn about it. That is our opinion. For a shop, a clinic, and most trades desks, the default is the product that already does the sentence, with a named person checking the output. Custom is the leftover, not a personality. We do not think building is a sign of ambition. We think building is what you do when the leftover is real and you can point at it without waving your hands.

We would make any builder repeat the miss before they give a price. We would make any shelf vendor handle yesterday's awkward job. We would keep the price, the clinic's scope, and the exception for a regular customer in human hands. The one exception is a product with a clear place to hold the rule, and a person who still checks the result. We would not let 58% or a revenue number choose for us. Those figures count use and reported boosts. They do not count your records.

If you are staring at a proposal this week, put it down and open the tool you already pay for. Try the job once, on purpose, with the person who will live with the result sitting next to you. If it works, you are finished, and finished is a good outcome. If it fails, you will have the sentence that any custom work has to honor. Either way, you will not have bought a custom frame just to impress a chart.

## What Is an AI Agent? A Plain Answer for Owners

An AI agent is a computer program that looks at what it just found and then picks its own next step. It stays inside limits that you set. A workflow is different, because it does the steps in an order that someone wrote down ahead of time. We use that split whenever an owner asks us if the new line on the invoice is a real agent or just a form with a louder name.

Anthropic's December 2024 essay draws the line the same way. In a workflow, large language models (the kind of AI that reads and writes text) follow a path that the builder set up. In an agent, the model directs its own process and decides which tools to use.[^anthropic] The essay also says to start with the simplest thing that works. Add more only when the simple version fails. We keep that advice on the table during these talks.

Most of the businesses we sit with are not stuck because their software is too plain. They are stuck because the work still lives in one person's memory. Then a seller asks a model to make up a process that nobody ever wrote down.

If the steps are still in someone's head, the [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-low) is the check that fits. The [use-case note](/blog/ai-agents-for-business) lists jobs that a system might take over. The [comparison note](/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai) stays on the words, which is where sales pages get slippery.

## When a workflow is enough

Use a workflow when you already know the steps. Think of taking an email, pulling out the details, writing a draft, and waiting for a person to look at it. Use an agent when the next step depends on what the last step found, and you cannot write down every branch ahead of time. If you cannot say when the system should stop, you do not really have either one yet.

Picture a plumbing desk on a loud Monday. The scheduler runs the book, so she gets the name, the address, and whether there is water on the floor. Then she asks which room it is in and whether anyone shut off the main. Those questions do not change just because a model showed up. A workflow can hold them in a form, a text to the on-call tech, and a line in the book. The fork comes after that intake, and it is the part people like to skip.

A restaurant with water coming through the ceiling is a very different promise from a slow drip under a rental sink. The restaurant needs the owner or the senior tech to say if someone rolls right now. The drip can wait for the afternoon route. Sellers offer an agent for that fork, one that reads the note and picks a tech, a part, and a time. We would let it draft the options. We would not let it text a time until the scheduler or the owner has looked. If the order is known, a workflow will do. If the order depends on what you just learned, an agent may help, and you still want a person who can stop the send.

<!--image:2-->

Here is how the three kinds of system compare. With one prompt, the person at the keyboard picks the next step, and it fits a single draft or a single answer. With a workflow, the path you wrote picks the next step, and it fits work where the steps rarely change. With an agent, the model picks the next step inside the limits you set, and it fits work where the path depends on what it finds.

Read that before you read any product page. With one prompt, the person is still choosing. They paste in the job notes, ask for a reply, and send it themselves, which can save a tired afternoon. That is not an agent, and it does not need to become one. A workflow means you know the order, and the software repeats it without getting bored or skipping the address. An agent means the model looks at what it found and picks a tool, such as the calendar, the parts list, or the text message. The limits are yours, because you decide which tools exist, what the system may never send, and who holds the stop.

That last test is the one we use with owners. If the steps rarely change, stop shopping and write down the path. If the path depends on what the system finds, you may want an agent. You still want the limits on one page that a new hire could follow. We have watched shops pay for an agent to do work that belongs in a simple workflow. Then the staff spends the week fixing a machine that was never supposed to decide anything.

## What the survey actually counts

Owners hear a loud number and think the whole trade has already moved past them. McKinsey's 2025 survey says that 88% of people report regular AI use in at least one part of their business, up from 78% a year earlier.[^mckinsey] That is a wide claim, because regular use can mean a person pasting a quote into a chat window on a Thursday. It is a very different thing from saying "we run an agent."

The numbers about agents are smaller, and they are the ones we want in the room. About 23% say their companies are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, and another 39% are trying agents out. In any single part of the business, no more than 10% say they are rolling out agents. Read that last number slowly. An agent somewhere in a big company is not the same as an agent running the scheduling desk. Companies that earn less than $100 million a year are less often at the wide rollout stage, at 29%. Nearly half of the companies that earn more than $5 billion are further along.

<!--cta:inline-->

Those are survey shares for big groups of companies. They are not a score for one small business. An agent still needs a written process and a person who can stop it.

We say this out loud because the big percentage gets used as a shove. A seller will put the 88% on a slide and talk as if a shop with a few trucks is running late. The survey does not say that. It says use is common, and rolling out an agent inside one team is not. If companies with real operations teams are mostly still trying things, you are allowed to write down your process first. You can do that before you buy a system that picks its own tools. The survey is a count of what people said. It is not a definition of an agent, and it is not a grade for your desk.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Stay with the plumbing desk and give everyone a job. This is a walk-through and not a result we measured. The owner takes the hard calls, a scheduler runs the book, and Luis and Priya work on the trucks.

A property manager calls about a smell in more than one unit. The scheduler opens the job the way she always does. She takes the name, a callback number, the address, the keys, and whether anyone is home. That part is a workflow, and it should not depend on a model's mood. Then the notes get messy. One unit had a dishwasher replaced not long ago, and another has a tenant who shuts off the water and tells nobody. A third unit is empty. The next step depends on what the scheduler just heard. Which door gets the first visit? Should the truck carry a camera? Is a smell in an empty unit a bigger problem than a clogged trap?

An agent, in the sense of that 2024 essay, could read the notes, look at the afternoon routes and the parts list, and suggest an order. It might send the empty unit first and put a camera on the truck. It might pick Luis because he did the camera work last week, while Priya is already on a job across town. The suggestion is the agent's work. The text to the manager is not, until the scheduler okays the words and the time. If the model cannot see the route, it should say so and stop. It should not make up an arrival window. A card by the phone says that no time goes out unless a person on the desk has tapped yes.

A workflow ends at the form. That is the right ending for intake, but it is the wrong tool for this fork, because you cannot write every branch of a messy call about many units ahead of time. A single prompt would mean the scheduler pastes the notes into a chat box and asks for a polite reply. That is fine on a quiet afternoon. But it does not watch the route, and it does not send anything.

The owner does not need a lecture on models. He needs to know which choices the desk may hand off. The scheduler needs "suggest" and "send" to be two different buttons. Luis needs the camera on his truck if the camera was the point. If none of them can point at the control that stops the system, you do not have an agent yet. You have a chat box wearing a job title, and the customer will hear its mistakes in your voice.

## How we'd run it

We would not start by picking software. We would sit with the scheduler and write down what she already does when the phone is mean.

First, name the job in one sentence that a new hire could repeat. For example, turn a call into a visit the tech can finish, without promising a time the route cannot keep. If that sentence grows into a whole menu, you have not named the job yet.

Second, write down the steps that never change. These are the name, the number, the address, the access, what is happening, and who is rolling. Use the scheduler's order and not a template's order. This workflow is the floor you build on, even if an agent comes later.

Third, mark the forks. A fork is any moment when the next step depends on what the last step found. It might be which unit to visit, whether to bring a camera, or whether the job is an emergency or can wait for the afternoon route. If you can write it as a rule, it is still a workflow. A rule like "water through the ceiling, page the owner" does not need a model.

Fourth, choose what the model may touch. We let it draft, suggest a tech, and suggest a part. We do not let it send, set a price, or say a word about who pays for damage. If the limit says "use your judgment," you have left a hole, and the model will fill it with something polite.

Fifth, name the stop and the person who holds it. The scheduler can stop it, the owner can stop it, and a tech can send back a job that came without the part. The system stops when a fact is missing, when a time falls outside the route, or when the caller is angry. Stopping is a good result and not a failure.

Sixth, replay recent jobs with the names covered up. The scheduler compares what the system suggested with what the desk actually did. She hunts for the time it sounded sure but was wrong. Fix the limits before a live customer sees a message. Only then should you try it on today's calls, with the send button still in a person's hand. We would repeat that replay until the refusals look right. We would not turn on automatic texts just because a free trial is ending.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is a new name on an old tool. The chat box gets called an agent because the invoice said so. But if a person still picks every next step, you have one prompt. That can be the right tool, yet the new name makes the staff expect judgment that the box does not have.

The second mistake is skipping the written path because writing feels slow. Then every exception becomes the model's problem, even the ones a card by the phone could handle. The staff stops trusting the book, and the scheduler goes back to her memory while you pay a fee on top.

The third mistake is a missing stop. The model may send texts, and nobody is named to halt it on a bad afternoon. The bad promise is usually small, like a time the tech cannot make. But the customer hears it as the business talking.

The fourth mistake is treating the survey as a target. Having 23% of companies rolling out an agent system somewhere is not a quota. Having 10% in any one part of the business is not a score you are failing. Chasing those shares just buys a tool that nobody can watch over.

The fifth mistake is letting the system near money. That means a price, a waived fee, or a line about whether the landlord pays. A draft that the owner edits is a very different thing from a message that has already gone out.

The sixth mistake is a limit written as a mood. "Be helpful" is not a limit. But "do not offer a same-day visit unless the owner has marked the job urgent" is one. If the scheduler cannot enforce the sentence, the model will be helpful in the wrong direction.

## What we'd do

We would write down the scheduler's path before we paid for anything that picks its own tools. We would use one prompt for the messy replies and a workflow for intake. We would use an agent only at the fork where the next visit depends on what the notes say. We would also keep the send button in a person's hand longer than a seller likes. Our view is plain. An agent is worth the trouble when the branch is real and a named person owns the stop. It is a poor buy when the process is still a story the owner tells at the counter.

The 2024 essay says to earn the extra complexity. The 2025 survey says that even large companies are mostly not rolling out agents inside any one team. We believe both. Then we go sit with the person who answers the phone, because that person already knows where the path breaks, and the software does not.

## What Is llms.txt, and Who Actually Reads It

llms.txt is a text file that someone proposed putting at the top level of a website. It lists the pages you most want an AI model to read, so think of it as a map. It is not a citation, and it does not change how you rank.

Jeremy Howard published the proposal in September 2024, and the page was updated in August 2026.[^llmstxt] The idea is a short list of pages for a model to read. It should be written so that a person can check it in one sitting. This site already has [its own file](/llms.txt), and that is a fact about this site, not a traffic number. We publish it because we like having a clean list of what we stand behind.

Google's guide says that Google does not use llms.txt for its AI features in search.[^google] We keep that next to the proposal, or the proposal turns into a rumor. A file that Google's AI features do not read cannot be the reason you show up in them. The page still has to be indexed, and it still has to deserve the quote.

To find out whether your file is missing, broken, or pointing at junk, use the [missing-file guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/missing-llms-txt) is the check. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) covers what Google does ask for, which is ordinary search work on a real page. The [GEO comparison](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) holds the research on being seen and getting the click.

## What a crawl of the files found

Ahrefs published a study in June 2026 that looked at 137,210 domains with website traffic in May 2026.[^ahrefs] About 28% of them had an llms.txt file, which came to about 38,000 valid files. Of those files, 97% got zero requests in May. Of the requests that did arrive, 96% came from bots. Named AI tools made up 19.5% of all requests, and audit or scanner tools made up 12%. We think those shares deserve a pause before you plan a project around the file. In that study most copies were never asked for. When something did ask, it was usually a bot, and only a smaller slice came from named AI tools.

We do not read this as a reason to never publish one. We read it as a reason not to expect the file to be a front door. A list that nobody asks for cannot fix a homepage that says nothing. A scanner asking for the list is not the same as a model citing you in an answer that a customer sees. The study counted requests against files, in one month, on sites that already had traffic. It is not a verdict on the idea, and it only tells us how often the file was fetched.

<!--image:2-->

<!--cta:inline-->

Publish the file if you want a clean list of your pages, but do not expect Google to read it. Keep your pages indexed and worth citing either way.

That is the order we use when we sit down with a client. Pages come first, then getting them indexed, then a sentence that a stranger can use. After that, if you still want the list, make a short file that points at those pages. Leave out drafts, tag dumps, and anything you would be ashamed to see quoted. The file is a courtesy and a way to keep control, but it is not the real work.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Take an independent bookshop. This is an example and not a study, so it has no score. A manager runs the floor and the website on the same tired afternoons. People ask, online and at the desk, for a book for a grieving friend. They ask for something a nine-year-old will really finish, and they ask whether tonight's reading is still on. The site has a homepage and an events page that is sometimes out of date. It also has a staff-picks page, which is the best thing they have written all year.

Someone on a forum told the manager that models will not understand the shop without llms.txt. So he made a long file. It linked every tag, every old event, and a draft page about a book club that never started. It looked thorough, but it was a bad map. A model that fetched it would have been sent to old nights and a club that does not exist. A model that never fetched it would have changed nothing, and that is the common case in the Ahrefs count. Either way, the manager would have spent his evening on the wrong thing.

If they publish a file, we would want it short. It would hold the staff-picks page. It would also hold the page that explains how to order a book the shop does not have on the shelf. It would hold the events page too, but only if the manager updates it whenever a reading is canceled. It would leave out the tag archives and the draft. The proposal, written in September 2024 and updated in August 2026, is a list of the pages you want read. The key word is "want." It does not mean everything the website software can produce.

Clear jobs keep the file honest. The owner decides which pages stand for the shop. If she would not hand a page to a regular, it stays off the list. The manager keeps the events page true, because a file that points at a lie is worse than no file. The real audience is not whoever fetches the file, or fails to fetch it. It is the person who needs a book this afternoon. So the staff-picks page has to work on its own, even if no model ever asks for the map. That is the lesson in the request counts. In the study, 97% of the valid files got zero requests in May 2026. A shop that only improved the file and left the picks page mushy would have improved the thing almost nobody asked for.

Google sits to the side of this scene on purpose. The guide says that Google does not use llms.txt for its AI features in search. So the owner could publish a lovely file and still be missing from those features. That happens if the picks page is thin, blocked, or hard to quote. The answer-engine work is the page, and the file is optional housekeeping. We would tell the manager that plainly. Then he will not buy a plugin that rebuilds the list every night from every web address it can see.

The mix of requests matters too, when someone waves a log at you. In that June 2026 study, 96% of the requests that did arrive came from bots. Named AI tools made up 19.5% of the requests, and audit or scanner tools made up 12%. A hit in a log is not a customer, since it is often a machine checking whether the file exists. Count a scanner hit as a scanner hit, and do not tell the owner it is demand.

## How we'd run it

We would first decide whether the list is worth keeping. Then we would write it by hand the first time.

First, pick the pages you hope a stranger finds, with the owner in the room. For the bookshop that means the staff picks and how to order a title the shop does not stock. It could also mean tonight's reading, but only if that page stays current. If you cannot name them without opening the website editor and scrolling, you are not ready to publish a map.

Second, make those pages good enough to quote with no file at all. They should be indexed, and they should open with clear lines. They should also have a sentence the manager would say at the desk. Google does not use the file for its AI features. So this step is the one that can affect that part of search. The [answer-engine note](/blog/answer-engine-optimization) says more about what good enough means. Please do not skip it just because a file feels more solid.

Third, write a short llms.txt that points only at those pages. Give each one a plain line of description that a person can check. Link the live address, and if the events page is out of date, leave it off until the manager fixes it. A short true list beats a long machine-made one. This site's own file was a choice of that kind, and it is not proof that files bring visits.

Fourth, put the file at the top level of the site, and then let go of the dream. Ahrefs looked at 137,210 domains with traffic in May 2026. It found that 28% had a file, about 38,000 valid ones, and 97% of those saw zero requests that month. If yours is in the quiet majority, the shop is not broken. The pages are still what matters.

Fifth, if you do watch your logs, tell machines apart from people. In the study, 96% of requests came from bots. Named AI tools made up 19.5%, and audit and scanner tools made up 12%. A spike from a scanner is not a crowd of readers, so do not rewrite the shop around it.

Sixth, look at the list again when the shop changes, and not on a timer. A new picks page, a book club that ended, or a reading series that wrapped up all count. The owner takes out the dead link that same week. A file that points at last year's calendar sends people the wrong way with total confidence. The August 2026 update of the proposal did not change that duty. The list should say what is true, or it should come down.

## Common mistakes

The first mistake is expecting Google to fetch it. The guide says Google does not use llms.txt for its AI features in search. So publishing one and waiting for AI answers is a plan the guide already turned down. Fix the page that Google can index instead.

The second mistake is a file made by a machine that dumps everything. Every tag, every attachment, and every draft ends up on it, but the proposal is a picked list. A dump hides the staff-picks page in noise, which is the opposite of pointing a model at your best work. It also goes stale, because nobody will look after a thousand automatic lines. We would rather the manager keep up a list that he can read aloud.

The third mistake is treating the Ahrefs shares as a personal failure or a trophy. Of those 137,210 domains, 28% had a file, which came to about 38,000 valid files, and 97% of them got zero requests in May 2026. You are not behind because you lack one. You are not ahead because you have one that nobody asked for. The study describes a crawl of files and says nothing about your customers.

The fourth mistake is reading bot traffic as people taking it up. Of the requests that arrived, 96% came from bots. Audit or scanner tools made up 12%, and named AI tools made up 19.5%. None of that says a reader found the shop, so call them machine requests or leave them out of the report.

The fifth mistake is letting the file disagree with the shop. Say the events page says Thursday, but the blurb in the file says Wednesday, copied from an old night. Whichever one gets quoted, you look careless. Keep the live page as the one place the facts live, and let the file follow it.

The sixth mistake is doing the file instead of the page because the file is smaller. A map to a vague homepage still leads to a vague homepage. The pages must be worth quoting whether or not anyone ever asks for the file. That is the plain lesson of a study where almost all valid files sat untouched for the month they measured.

## What we'd do

We would publish a short file only after the pages are true. We would not tell the owner it will bring her readers. Our view is that the proposal is a fair courtesy and a poor priority. September 2024 is when the idea was written down, and August 2026 is when the page was updated. In June 2026 a large study of 137,210 domains found that 97% of valid files got zero requests. It also found that 96% of the requests that did show up came from bots. A courtesy is allowed to be quiet, but a plan is not allowed to ignore a quiet result.

Google has said it does not use the file. So we would spend the manager's evening on the staff-picks page, the ordering page, and an events page that survives a canceled reading. Then we would add a list of those addresses if the owner likes to see what the shop stands behind in one place. We would keep our own file for that same reason, and we would never wave it around as proof of traffic. A file is a pointer, and the page is what a person came for. If you only have time for one, choose the page. The pointer can wait until the page can stand on its own.

## Why AI Pilots Stall After the Demo

An AI pilot stalls when the demo works but the daily work never does. Everyone liked what they saw in the meeting. Then Monday came, and the pilot hit real files, real handoffs, and a person who could say no.

In January 2026, Gartner wrote that at least 50% of generative AI projects were dropped after the first test run. The reasons were poor data, weak risk controls, costs that kept growing, and unclear value.[^gartner-fail] We read that list as a plain checklist. If any of those four is blank for your pilot, it is already sliding toward the dropped pile, even if nobody has said so yet.

Our [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-low) fits this problem best. The steps that should come before a demo are in our [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework). The trouble we see most often is in our [data note](/blog/ai-ready-data). A pilot that cannot point to the one place its facts live is not early. It is unfinished, and paying for another demo will not finish it.

We have sat through the awkward meeting that follows a nice demo. The owner feels embarrassed, and the staff are tired of sample data. Someone suggests a new vendor, as if the vendor were the missing piece. The vendor was never missing. What was missing was a decision.

## Using AI is not the same as rolling it out

McKinsey's 2025 survey found that 88% of people use AI regularly in at least one part of their business. A year earlier, that number was 78%.[^mckinsey] About one third of companies are rolling AI out widely. Only 23% are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, and 39% are still trying things out. No more than 10% are rolling out agents in any single part of the business. Among companies that earn less than $100 million a year, 29% have reached the wide rollout stage. Among companies that earn more than $5 billion, it is nearly half.

Those numbers describe a stalled pilot well. Use grew fast, but only a small group of companies can run a tool every day inside one team. A small company should not hear the big-company numbers as a dare. Even the very large firms work in a different way than a dispatcher and an owner do. Your pilot may be stuck because of your own files, and that has nothing to do with how big you are.

<!--image:2-->

In June 2025, Gartner said that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027.[^gartner-agentic] We read that as a warning about projects that never became a daily habit. It does not say the software is bad. Projects get canceled when the cost, the value, or the checking stays vague after the demo. We would rather you stop a pilot on purpose this month than let it drift into that pile and blame bad luck.

<!--cta:inline-->

Say a pilot cannot name its data, the person who checks it, and the value it brings. Then it is already in the dropped pile. Turn it into a written routine, or stop it. A third choice, like waiting to see how the next demo feels, is how the same bill keeps coming back.

<!--image:3-->

## A worked example

Picture a small electrical company. This story is made up, and we did not measure it. The owner still prices the odd jobs herself. A dispatcher plans the day's routes. Two technicians send photos from the job site. An office lead turns those photos and the customers' texts into a quote whenever she can get the owner's attention.

The company paid for a pilot that turns incoming texts into a tidy intake note. In the demo, the seller pasted in three clean conversations. The note came back with the address, the problem, and a next step. Everyone nodded, and the owner pictured the office lead going home on time.

Monday looked nothing like the demo. One customer changed the light fixture in a later text. Then the same customer sent a photo of the old fixture by mistake and asked if the price included the permit. The job history lived in a group chat that the pilot could not see. The price list was a spreadsheet on the owner's laptop, named in a way only she could remember. The office lead could not tell if a summary was safe to send, because the note never said which messages it had skipped.

The data was poor in a clear way. The facts lived in many places, and the pilot acted as if they lived in one. Nobody was named to stop a quote that sounded sure but was wrong. The cost started as a small monthly fee. Then it grew when the seller offered a second task while they were already set up. The value had been described as saving the office lead's afternoon. But nobody had written down what that would look like on a Thursday when the phones were awful.

So the pilot stalled at the handoff, which is where most pilots stall. The demo had no handoff, because it ended at the summary. The real work ended when a person had to put the company's name on that summary. The office lead stopped trusting it, yet the tab stayed open. The owner kept paying, because canceling felt like admitting the demo had fooled her. It had not fooled her. It had shown her a different company, one with clean message threads and a price list the software could read.

## How we'd run it

We do not try to bring a stalled pilot back with a pep talk. We make a short decision in a set order, and we are fine if the answer is to stop.

First, we write down the original promise in one sentence. We use the words the owner remembers from the sales meeting. For the electrical company, it might be that the office lead gets an intake note she can trust from the customers' texts. If nobody can write that sentence, the pilot never had a job to do. We stop there and say so out loud, because vague hope is not worth another month of payments.

Second, we turn the four reasons projects get dropped into questions, not blame. Is the data good enough to back up the sentence? In this office, can the note see the whole message thread, the right photo, and the price list? Are the risk controls real, meaning we know who may send a quote and who must stop one? Is the cost still the cost you agreed to, or did it pick up a second task? Is the value clear enough that the office lead would notice if it went away? Any blank answer is a good reason to pause the spending.

Third, we pick the person who checks the work before we talk about a better prompt. In this office, the checker is the office lead. The owner backs her up on jobs above the dollar line they already use for quotes done by hand. If nobody can name that person, the pilot is only a toy. We also sit with her and watch her handle one real message thread. Watching can bruise the seller's story, but it is very kind to the business.

Fourth, we choose a written routine or a stop, and we do it in the same meeting. A written routine says which places the note may pull from. It names the message thread, the photo rule, and the price list, and the office lead still sends every quote. A stop means the subscription ends. The one-sentence promise goes into a folder until the price list lives somewhere more than one person can find it. We do not book a second demo with cleaner samples, because cleaner samples are how the first meeting gave a false picture.

Fifth, we tell the staff about the decision in plain words. If we keep the pilot, they hear what will change on Monday. If we stop it, they hear that stopping was the plan and that it says nothing bad about the office lead. People will keep feeding a dead pilot if they think the owner is ashamed. Shame costs a lot of money, and a clear sentence costs almost nothing.

## Common mistakes

Calling the stall a delay is a polite way of not telling the truth. The dispatcher says the team is still rolling it out. A real rollout has a date and a named person. A stall has an open tab and a bad feeling. If the office lead has quietly gone back to the old message thread, you are not late. You have already picked the old way, and you are paying twice, once in money and once in pretending.

Blaming the AI model for facts that live in many places wastes the next month. The summary was shaky because the price list sat in a private file and the photo did not match the text. A newer model will sound even more sure about the same gap. Sounding sure is not the same as knowing. We have watched owners swap tools and repeat the same stall with better grammar.

Letting the seller decide what counts as value is how costs creep up. Time back is not real value until the office lead agrees on which hour comes back and what she will do with it. If she says she will finally eat lunch, believe her. Then check whether the note really gives her that lunch. If the note adds a new review chore that eats the same lunch, the value was only a slogan.

Skipping risk controls because it is just office work is how a bad quote leaves the building. Office work is your voice to your customers. A wrong intake note turns into a wrong visit, a wrong part, and a customer who thinks you never listen. The control has to be a named person. A box in the software that says a human will check does not help if nobody's day includes that check.

Paying for a fresh demo to avoid the stop talk is the costly mistake. Gartner's June 2025 forecast says that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. This habit is what that looks like across many companies. You can be a project that ends with a clear reason, or one that ends later after a longer bill. We would rather you take the shorter bill.

## What we'd do

We would score the stalled pilot before we let anyone pay for another demo. That is a strong opinion, and we stand by it. A second demo feels hopeful, but it is usually a way to avoid telling the seller and the staff that the first promise had no data behind it. The [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-low) is the page we open in that meeting. If the score says the business is not ready to decide, we still decide. Not being ready is a good reason to stop spending.

We would not comfort a small company with the McKinsey usage number. Saying that 88% use AI regularly, up from 78% a year earlier, only tells you people opened a tool. It does not tell you the office lead trusts a quote. About one third of companies are rolling AI out widely, 23% are rolling out an agent system somewhere, and 39% are still trying things out. No more than 10% are rolling out agents in any one part of the business. That is the honest picture. And 29% of firms under $100 million in revenue have reached wide rollout, against nearly half of firms over $5 billion. So the middle is hard even before you count being small. Being small is not what stalls a pilot. A missing checker is.

We would also do the data work first, every time. That is why we send owners to the [data note](/blog/ai-ready-data) before we ever talk about prompts. If they decide to go on, the order of the steps is in the [implementation framework](/blog/ai-implementation-framework). It does not call for a new pilot with a new logo. Our bet is simple. A stopped pilot with a written reason makes a healthier company than a live pilot that nobody will sign their name to.
